style="color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b>?</b></font>" help="Scheduler & Controller Manager > API Server

The kube-scheduler and kube-controller-manager act as clients of the Kubernetes API and initiate authenticated HTTPS connections to the API server.

Both use list/watch requests to continuously observe cluster state and write changes back through the API. The scheduler assigns pods to nodes, while the controller-manager reconciles resources toward their desired state.

All requests are authenticated and authorized by the API server. Neither component accesses etcd directly." tags="level-2 info Api ControlPlane _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="CoreToApi" id="2NIop3rW37v0lhN0G3K2-65"> <mxCell parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;arcSize=10;fillColor=#DFF4FF;strokeColor=#0B6FA4;strokeWidth=1;fontColor=#0A3D5A;rotation=0;opacity=80;shadow=0;glass=0;labelBorderColor=none;textShadow=1;html=1;fontSize=9;spacing=2;" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="17" width="17" x="20" y="-160" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="<font style="color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b>?</b></font>" help="The kube-controller-manager runs the core controllers responsible for continuously reconciling the desired state stored in Kubernetes with the observed state of the cluster.

It contains multiple independent control loops, including controllers for Nodes, ReplicaSets, Deployments, Jobs, Namespaces, ServiceAccounts, and many other Kubernetes resources.

Controllers continuously list and watch resources through the Kubernetes API.

When the observed state differs from the desired state, they create, update, or delete resources through the API to move the cluster toward the desired state. They do not communicate directly with the scheduler, kubelet, or etcd.

The controller-manager operates using its own authenticated identity and requires broad cluster-wide API permissions because its controllers manage many different resource types.

From a security perspective, the controller-manager is one of the most privileged control-plane components. Compromise of its identity or credentials can provide extensive control over cluster resources, making protection of its credentials, configuration, and host particularly important." tags="level-2 info ControlPlane ControlPlane.ControllerManager _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="ControllerManager" id="2NIop3rW37v0lhN0G3K2-67"> <mxCell parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;arcSize=10;fillColor=#DFF4FF;strokeColor=#0B6FA4;strokeWidth=1;fontColor=#0A3D5A;rotation=0;opacity=80;shadow=0;glass=0;labelBorderColor=none;textShadow=1;html=1;fontSize=9;spacing=2;" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="17" width="17" x="-90" y="-150" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="<font style="color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b>?</b></font>" help="Kube-Scheduler

The kube-scheduler is responsible for selecting which node should run each newly created Pod that has not yet been assigned to a node.

It continuously watches the Kubernetes API for unscheduled Pods and maintains information about Nodes and other resources required to make scheduling decisions. It considers available resources, scheduling constraints, affinity, taints and tolerations, topology, and other scheduling policies.

Once a node has been selected, the scheduler records the decision through the Kubernetes API. It does not communicate directly with the kubelet or etcd.

The scheduler operates using its own authenticated identity and requires cluster-wide read access to several resources, while its write permissions are primarily related to scheduling Pods. Its API access is controlled through Kubernetes authorization, typically RBAC.

From a security perspective, the scheduler is highly trusted because it can influence where workloads execute. However, its API privileges are generally more limited than those of the kube-controller-manager." tags="level-2 info ControlPlane ControlPlane.Scheduler _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="Scheduler" id="2NIop3rW37v0lhN0G3K2-68"> <mxCell parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;arcSize=10;fillColor=#DFF4FF;strokeColor=#0B6FA4;strokeWidth=1;fontColor=#0A3D5A;rotation=0;opacity=80;shadow=0;glass=0;labelBorderColor=none;textShadow=1;html=1;fontSize=9;spacing=2;" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="17" width="17" x="-119" y="-151" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="<font style="font-size: 18px; color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b style="">?</b></font>" help="Kubernetes Resources

Kubernetes resources are API objects that describe the desired or observed state of the cluster. Examples include Pods, Deployments, Services, Secrets, Nodes, Roles, and NetworkPolicies.

Resources can be created by users and applications through the Kubernetes API, or automatically by controllers and other Kubernetes components. Controllers continuously watch resources and may create, modify, or delete other resources to reconcile the cluster toward its desired state.

Namespaced resources belong to a specific namespace and are commonly used for workloads and their configuration. Examples include Pods, Deployments, Services, Secrets, ConfigMaps, and Roles.

Cluster-scoped resources exist across the entire cluster and do not belong to a namespace. Examples include Nodes, Namespaces, ClusterRoles, StorageClasses, and PersistentVolumes.

All resources are accessed and managed through the Kubernetes API, where authentication, authorization, admission control, and other security controls determine who can perform operations on them." tags="info legend" slug="K8sResources" id="2NIop3rW37v0lhN0G3K2-69"> <mxCell parent="1" </object> <UserObject label="" help="Cloud-Native Application Protection Platform (CNAPP)

A CNAPP provides centralized security visibility and protection across Kubernetes, containers, cloud infrastructure, and workloads.

It typically combines vulnerability and image scanning, security posture management, identity and permission analysis, compliance monitoring, and runtime threat detection.

A CNAPP helps identify and prioritize risks across multiple security layers instead of evaluating vulnerabilities and misconfigurations in isolation.

Examples:
Wiz, Sysdig, Prisma Cloud, and Aqua Security.

Open-source building blocks:
Kubescape, Trivy, Falco and NeuVector, some of them for just scanning images for vulnerabilities in a remote repository." tags="level-1 pri-2 Cnapp" slug="Cnapp" id="2NIop3rW37v0lhN0G3K2-91"> <mxCell parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fillColor=#FFD1A1;strokeColor=#B45F06;rounded=1;strokeWidth=3;align=center;verticalAlign=middle;arcSize=10;fontFamily=Helvetica;fontSize=12;fontColor=#6B2F00;rotation=0;opacity=80;" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="20" width="20" x="-243" y="444" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="<font style="color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b>?</b></font>" help="NodePort

A NodePort exposes a Service on a static port on every Kubernetes node.

Traffic sent to <NodeIP>:<NodePort> is forwarded by the Kubernetes networking implementation to one of the Service's backend Pods.

NodePort provides basic external reachability, but does not itself provision an external load balancer or public IP." tags="level-3 info Network Network.Ingress Ingress Ingress.Controller _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="NodePort" id="2NIop3rW37v0lhN0G3K2-95"> <mxCell parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;arcSize=10;fillColor=#DFF4FF;strokeColor=#0B6FA4;strokeWidth=1;fontColor=#0A3D5A;rotation=0;opacity=80;shadow=0;glass=0;labelBorderColor=none;textShadow=1;html=1;fontSize=9;spacing=2;" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="14" width="18" x="939" y="-154" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="<font style="color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b>?</b></font>" help="LoadBalancer

A LoadBalancer Service requests an external load balancer from an integrated cloud provider or load-balancer implementation such as MetalLB.

The load balancer receives an external IP and forwards traffic into the Kubernetes Service, which then distributes traffic to its backend Pods.

A LoadBalancer Service typically builds on the same Service mechanisms as NodePort, although implementations may route traffic differently and can bypass NodePort." tags="level-3 info Network Network.Ingress Ingress Ingress.GatewayApi Ingress.GatewayApi.Gateway _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="LoadBalancer" help.yaml.fixed_loadbalancer_ip="# Asks MetalLB for a fixed IP; externalTrafficPolicy Local keeps the client source IP
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
 name: ingress-nginx-controller
 namespace: ingress-nginx
 annotations:
 metallb.io/loadBalancerIPs: 10.20.8.20
spec:
 type: LoadBalancer
 externalTrafficPolicy: Local
 selector:
 app.kubernetes.io/name: ingress-nginx
 ports:
 - name: https
 port: 443
 targetPort: https" id="2NIop3rW37v0lhN0G3K2-96"> <mxCell parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;arcSize=10;fillColor=#DFF4FF;strokeColor=#0B6FA4;strokeWidth=1;fontColor=#0A3D5A;rotation=0;opacity=80;shadow=0;glass=0;labelBorderColor=none;textShadow=1;html=1;fontSize=9;spacing=2;" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="14" width="18" x="938" y="-133" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="<font style="color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b>?</b></font>" help="NodePort Exposure

By default, Kubernetes reserves ports 30000-32767 for NodePort Services.
A NodePort is normally exposed on eligible network interfaces of every node, meaning <NodeIP>:<NodePort> can provide an entry point to the Service.

The port range can be changed using the kube-apiserver option:
--service-node-port-range=30000-32767

Which node addresses accept NodePort traffic can be restricted using the kube-proxy --nodeport-addresses option. This allows NodePort to bind only to selected node networks, for example an internal network.

Network firewalls should additionally restrict access to the NodePort range from untrusted networks.

Note: CNI implementations such as Cilium may implement NodePort without kube-proxy and provide their own configuration for controlling exposure." tags="level-3 info Network Network.Ingress Ingress Ingress.Controller" slug="NodePortExposure" help.shell.list_nodeport_services="# Every NodePort Service opens its port on all nodes; list them
$ kubectl get svc -A --field-selector spec.type=NodePort
NAMESPACE NAME TYPE CLUSTER-IP EXTERNAL-IP PORT(S) AGE

To keep the argocd that deals with platform and infrastructure separate from application is good practice. The argocd that deploy the developer applications shoulnt have access to the service-accounts that handles cluster-wide and important resources." tags="level-2 pri-2 SupplyChain SupplyChain.Gitops _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="ArgocdOwner" help.yaml.restrict_team_project="# Team project: only its repo, only namespace shop, no cluster resources, no RBAC/quota/netpol
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AppProject
metadata:
 name: shop
 namespace: argocd
spec:
 sourceRepos:
 - https://git.fjordmart.example/shop/deploy.git
 destinations:
 - server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
 namespace: shop
 clusterResourceWhitelist: []
 namespaceResourceBlacklist:
 - group: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
 kind: Role
 - group: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
 kind: RoleBinding
 - group: ""
 kind: ResourceQuota
 - group: ""
 kind: LimitRange
 - group: networking.k8s.io
 kind: NetworkPolicy
---
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
 name: shop
 namespace: argocd
spec:
 project: shop
 source:
 repoURL: https://git.fjordmart.example/shop/deploy.git
 targetRevision: main
 path: overlays/k8s-prod
 destination:
 server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
 namespace: shop
 syncPolicy:
 automated:
 prune: true
 selfHeal: true" id="2NIop3rW37v0lhN0G3K2-135"> <mxCell parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fillColor=#FFD1A1;strokeColor=#B45F06;rounded=1;strokeWidth=3;align=center;verticalAlign=middle;arcSize=10;fontFamily=Helvetica;fontSize=12;fontColor=#6B2F00;rotation=0;opacity=80;" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="20" width="20" x="-6" y="-198" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="" help="Argocd (operator)

The argocd used by the platform team should be running on a separate cluster. It contains credentials with admin privileges to the cluster it manages. Thats why we run it outside the cluster, so nothing inside the cluster can access it." tags="level-2 pri-2 SupplyChain SupplyChain.Gitops _ _.Area _.Area.PlatformManagement" slug="ArgocdPlatform" For git operations that can have big impact, there should be "4-eyes" before the change is live.
This can be done with protected branches, but also signing of the git-repo itself using tools like gittuf." tags="level-3 pri-3 SupplyChain SupplyChain.Git SupplyChain.Gitops _ _.Area _.Area.PlatformManagement" slug="FourEyes" help.shell.require_two_signatures_with_gittuf="# gittuf: changes to main need signatures from 2 of 3 people; every clone can verify it, not only the git forge
$ gittuf policy add-person -k keys/policy --person-ID mdahl --public-key keys/mdahl.pub
$ gittuf policy add-person -k keys/policy --person-ID jberg --public-key keys/jberg.pub
$ gittuf policy add-person -k keys/policy --person-ID ihagen --public-key keys/ihagen.pub
$ gittuf policy add-rule -k keys/policy --rule-name protect-main --rule-pattern git:refs/heads/main --authorize mdahl --authorize jberg --authorize ihagen --threshold 2
$ gittuf policy stage --local-only
$ gittuf policy apply --local-only
# main has a new commit signed only by mdahl
$ gittuf verify-ref main
Error: verifying Git namespace policies failed, gittuf policy verification failed" help.json.protect_main_branch="# Forgejo: no direct push to main, 2 approvals, signed commits, also for admins
$ curl -X POST https://git.fjordmart.example/api/v1/repos/shop/deploy/branch_protections -H "Authorization: token $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @-
{
 "rule_name": "main",
 "enable_push": false,
 "required_approvals": 2,
 "dismiss_stale_approvals": true,
 "block_on_rejected_reviews": true,
 "block_on_outdated_branch": true,
 "require_signed_commits": true,
 "apply_to_admins": true
}" id="2NIop3rW37v0lhN0G3K2-147"> <mxCell parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fillColor=#FFF2A6;strokeColor=#B68A00;rounded=1;strokeWidth=3;align=center;verticalAlign=middle;arcSize=10;fontFamily=Helvetica;fontSize=12;fontColor=#5C4300;rotation=0;opacity=80;" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="20" width="20" x="-458" y="19" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="" help="Image Builder

The image builder produces trusted artifacts and must maintain verifiable build provenance.
Each image should be linked to its source commit, build identity, SBOM, and resulting image digest.

Build provenance and attestations should be signed and stored in an append-only transparency log, such as Sigstore Rekor, allowing the origin and integrity of deployed images to be independently verified." tags="level-3 pri-3 SupplyChain SupplyChain.ImageBuild _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="ImageBuilder" help.containerfile.multi_stage_nonroot_build="# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
# Build in a Go image, ship only the static binary on distroless, running as UID 65532
FROM registry.fjordmart.example/base/go:1.24 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o /out/storefront ./cmd/storefront

FROM registry.fjordmart.example/base/distroless-static:nonroot
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source="https://git.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront"
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.version="2.8.1"
USER 65532:65532
COPY --from=build /out/storefront /usr/local/bin/storefront
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/storefront"]" id="2NIop3rW37v0lhN0G3K2-148"> <mxCell parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fillColor=#FFF2A6;strokeColor=#B68A00;rounded=1;strokeWidth=3;align=center;verticalAlign=middle;arcSize=10;fontFamily=Helvetica;fontSize=12;fontColor=#5C4300;rotation=0;opacity=80;" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="20" width="20" x="-51" y="346" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="" help="User Namespace

Linux user namespaces isolate user and group identities between a container and the host.

UIDs and GIDs inside the namespace can be mapped to different IDs outside it. This allows UID 0 (root) inside a container to be mapped to an unprivileged UID on the host.

In Kubernetes, this isolation can be enabled for a pod using hostUsers: false, which automatically assigns and manages the UID/GID mapping.

This provides an additional isolation boundary and limits the privileges of container processes on the host." tags="level-3 pri-1 ProcessSecurity ProcessSecurity.Namespaces _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod _.Area.Container _.Area.Process _.Area.OsNamespaces" slug="UserNamespace" help.shell.check_uid_mapping="# hostUsers: false: UID 0 in the container is UID 833617920 on the host
$ kubectl exec -n shop storefront-6c9fd4d8b7-x2n4k -- cat /proc/self/uid_map
 0 833617920 65536
# hostUsers: true (default): container UIDs are host UIDs
$ kubectl exec -n shop cache-warmer -- cat /proc/self/uid_map
 0 0 4294967295" id="2NIop3rW37v0lhN0G3K2-150"> <mxCell parent="1" height="16" width="55" x="172" y="417" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="" help="Virtual Machine Resources

The resources visible to the guest are virtual hardware provided by QEMU/KVM and configured through the VirtualMachine specification.

vCPUs are backed by QEMU execution threads scheduled on host CPUs, while virtual memory is backed by memory allocated to the virt-launcher pod. Virtual disks are typically backed by PVCs or DataVolumes, and virtual NICs are connected through the pod's networking or additional network attachments.

KubeVirt translates the VM configuration into the required pod resources, devices and runtime configuration. Kubernetes cgroups and resource limits therefore still control the underlying host resources available to the VM." tags="level-1 pri-3 Workload Workload.Vm _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.VirtualMachine _.Area.VmPod _.Area.VmProcess" slug="VmResources" id="2NIop3rW37v0lhN0G3K2-158"> <mxCell parent="1" Inter-node traffic may use direct IP-to-IP communication or be encapsulated, depending on the CNI configuration. Encryption can be applied at this level via service mesh (e.g., mTLS) or CNI-level encryption.

Certain workloads—such as ingress controllers, operators, or AI/ML jobs—should be scheduled on dedicated nodes using taints, tolerations, or node selectors to enforce separation and reduce security risk.

There can be many different types of nodes." tags="level-2 pri-3 Node Node.Roles" slug="OtherNodes" id="2NIop3rW37v0lhN0G3K2-213"> <mxCell parent="1" target="2NIop3rW37v0lhN0G3K2-226"> <mxGeometry relative="1" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </object> <UserObject label="" help="SBOM

A Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) provides a machine-readable inventory of the components and dependencies contained in an image.

It enables continuous vulnerability assessment, license tracking, and rapid identification of affected workloads when new vulnerabilities are discovered.

SBOMs should be generated during the build, associated with the image digest, and stored alongside the artifact using standards such as SPDX or CycloneDX." tags="level-3 pri-3 SupplyChain SupplyChain.Sbom _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="Sbom" help.shell.generate_sbom="# List what is in the image, then attach the SPDX SBOM to it as a signed attestation
$ syft registry:registry.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront:2.8.1 -o spdx-json=storefront.spdx.json
$ syft registry:registry.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront:2.8.1
NAME VERSION TYPE
base-files 12.4+deb12u15 deb
ca-certificates 20250419~deb12u1 deb
media-types 10.0.0 deb
netbase 6.4 deb
stdlib go1.24.13 go-module
tzdata 2026b-0+deb12u1 deb
$ cosign attest --key hashivault://shop-images --type spdxjson --predicate storefront.spdx.json registry.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront@sha256:3c9e1f7a5b2d48e06a1c9f3b7d5e2a084f6c1b9d3e7a5f20c8b4d6e1a9f3c7b2" id="2NIop3rW37v0lhN0G3K2-230"> <mxCell parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fillColor=#FFF2A6;strokeColor=#B68A00;rounded=1;strokeWidth=3;align=center;verticalAlign=middle;arcSize=10;fontFamily=Helvetica;fontSize=12;fontColor=#5C4300;rotation=0;opacity=80;" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="20" width="20" x="-124" y="267" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="" help="Provenance / Attestation

Provenance describes where an artifact came from and how it was produced, while attestations provide verifiable claims about the artifact and its build process.

Attestations can link an image digest to its source commit, build system, dependencies, SBOM, and security checks, creating a verifiable chain from source to deployment.

They should be cryptographically signed and verified before deployment, ensuring that only artifacts produced through trusted build processes are allowed to run." tags="level-3 pri-3 SupplyChain SupplyChain.Signing _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="Provenance" help.json.provenance_attestation="# SLSA build provenance attached to the image, decoded (trimmed)
$ cosign verify-attestation --key hashivault://shop-images --type slsaprovenance1 registry.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront@sha256:3c9e1f7a5b2d48e06a1c9f3b7d5e2a084f6c1b9d3e7a5f20c8b4d6e1a9f3c7b2 | jq -r .payload | base64 -d

 }

Use a CNI plugin that supports fine-grained network policies and visibility, such as Cilium with eBPF. Define a baseline deny-all policy and explicitly allow only required traffic.

Deploy network observability tooling that can provide workload-aware visibility into network flows, policy verdicts, and DNS activity.

Retain flow telemetry centrally to enable historical correlation between network indicators and Kubernetes workloads during incident investigation.

Network observability complements network policy enforcement but does not replace it." tags="level-3 pri-2 Node Node.Observability Node.Observability.Hubble _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.NodeContext" slug="Hubble" help.log.dns_flows="$ hubble observe --protocol dns

x="-3" y="685" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="" help="Runtime Security and Observability (e.g., Tetragon, Falco)

Use runtime security tooling to observe process execution, system calls, network connections, and other security-relevant activity inside workloads.

Correlate runtime events with Kubernetes metadata to identify which process, container, and workload caused suspicious activity.

Runtime visibility provides context that network telemetry alone cannot provide." tags="level-3 pri-2 Node Node.RuntimeSecurity _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.NodeContext _.Area.RuntimeInstrumentation" slug="RuntimeSecurity" id="2NIop3rW37v0lhN0G3K2-248"> <mxCell parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fillColor=#FFD1A1;strokeColor=#B45F06;rounded=1;strokeWidth=3;align=center;verticalAlign=middle;arcSize=10;fontFamily=Helvetica;fontSize=12;rotation=0;opacity=80;fontColor=#6B2F00;" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="20" width="20" x="-14" y="794" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="" help="Runtime Security (e.g., Tetragon)

Use eBPF-based runtime security to observe and control process execution, network activity, and other kernel-level behavior with Kubernetes workload context.

Tracing policies can provide targeted visibility and enforcement for security-sensitive runtime activity." tags="level-3 pri-2 Node Node.RuntimeSecurity _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.NodeContext _.Area.RuntimeInstrumentation" slug="Tetragon" help.log.process_events="$ kubectl -n kube-system logs tetragon-p8x2z -c export-stdout | tetra getevents -o compact --pods cache-warmer
🚀 process shop/cache-warmer /bin/sh -c "echo f0VMRgIBAQAAAAAAAAAAAAIAPgABAAAA[…] | base64 -d > /tmp/.kworkerd && chmod +x /tmp/.kworkerd && /tmp/.kworkerd -d t.cdnx.example"
🚀 process shop/cache-warmer /usr/bin/base64 -d
💥 exit shop/cache-warmer /usr/bin/base64 -d 0
🚀 process shop/cache-warmer /usr/bin/chmod +x /tmp/.kworkerd
💥 exit shop/cache-warmer /usr/bin/chmod +x /tmp/.kworkerd 0
🚀 process shop/cache-warmer /tmp/.kworkerd -d t.cdnx.example" id="2NIop3rW37v0lhN0G3K2-249"> <mxCell parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fillColor=#FFD1A1;strokeColor=#B45F06;rounded=1;strokeWidth=3;align=center;verticalAlign=middle;arcSize=10;fontFamily=Helvetica;fontSize=12;rotation=0;opacity=80;fontColor=#6B2F00;" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="20" width="20" x="-18" y="820" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="" help="Runtime Threat Detection (e.g., Falco)

Use runtime threat detection to identify suspicious behavior such as unexpected process execution, privilege changes, sensitive file access, and unusual network activity.

Tune detection rules to the expected behavior of workloads and forward alerts to a central security monitoring system." tags="level-3 pri-2 Node Node.RuntimeSecurity _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.NodeContext _.Area.RuntimeInstrumentation" slug="Falco" help.yaml.dropped_binary_rule="- rule: Dropped binary executed in container
 desc: A process started from a file written after the container started
 condition: >
 spawned_process and container
 and proc.is_exe_upper_layer = true
 output: >
 Dropped binary executed (exe=%proc.exepath cmdline=%proc.cmdline user=%user.name
 pod=%k8s.ns.name/%k8s.pod.name image=%container.image.repository digest=%container.image.digest)
 priority: CRITICAL
 tags: [container, process, mitre_execution, TA0002]" help.json.dropped_binary_alert="$ kubectl -n falco logs falco-7tq9d -c falco | grep 'Dropped binary' | jq -S '{time, rule, priority, hostname, output_fields}'

Node-level controls can provide visibility and enforcement across workloads, including network datapaths, process execution, system calls, and other kernel-observable activity." tags="level-3 info Node _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="NodeSecurity" help.shell.node_level_agents="# Node-level security agents run as DaemonSets: one pod per node

help="Security Logging and Monitoring

Kubernetes security-relevant logs should be collected centrally and forwarded to a remote logging or SIEM platform such as Splunk for monitoring, correlation, alerting, and long-term retention.

Important sources include Kubernetes API audit logs, control-plane component logs, kubelet and container runtime logs, authentication and authorization events, admission controller decisions, CNI/network security logs, and security events generated by runtime detection tools.

Kubernetes Audit Logging is particularly important because it records requests made to the Kubernetes API, including who performed an action, which resource was accessed or modified, and whether the request was allowed or denied.

Logs should be stored outside the cluster or otherwise protected from workloads and compromised nodes to prevent attackers from modifying or deleting security evidence." tags="level-1 pri-2 Logging" slug="SecurityLogging" help.yaml.audit_policy="# kube-apiserver --audit-policy-file: metadata for secrets/configmaps, full request/response for pod and RBAC changes
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
omitStages: ["RequestReceived"]
rules:
 - level: None
 users: ["system:kube-proxy"]
 verbs: ["watch"]
 - level: Metadata
 resources:
 - group: ""
 resources: ["secrets", "configmaps", "serviceaccounts/token"]
 - level: RequestResponse
 verbs: ["create", "patch", "update", "delete"]
 resources:
 - group: ""
 resources: ["pods", "pods/exec", "pods/ephemeralcontainers"]
 - group: "rbac.authorization.k8s.io"
 - level: Metadata" help.json.pod_create_audit_event="# Audit event: ServiceAccount storefront creates pod cache-warmer (request/response bodies left out)

<UserObject label="<font style="font-size: 18px; color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b style="">?</b></font>" help="Multi-interface (Multus)

A pod can have multiple network interfaces using the Multus CNI plugin.
This allows attaching additional networks to a pod beyond the default CNI.

It is useful for scenarios like separating control and data planes, connecting to legacy networks, or assigning dedicated interfaces for specific protocols." tags="level-3 info Network Network.Cni Network.Cni.Multus _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod" slug="Multus" id="O8AOIrqbN8MiM61wshBk-18"> <mxCell parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;arcSize=10;fillColor=#DFF4FF;strokeColor=#0B6FA4;strokeWidth=3;fontColor=#0A3D5A;rotation=0;opacity=80;shadow=0;glass=0;labelBorderColor=none;textShadow=1;html=1;" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="20" width="26" x="629" y="542" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="" help="Network interfaces (underlay)

Pods can use different types of network interfaces depending on requirements.
Containers can bind directly to the host interface, or use other means to communicate over vlans and such.

Be aware: underlay networks (e.g., macvlan) typically bypass Kubernetes NetworkPolicies.
Overlay networks used by most CNIs enforce policy as expected and are safer by default." tags="level-3 pri-2 Network Network.Cni _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod" slug="Underlay" id="O8AOIrqbN8MiM61wshBk-19"> <mxCell parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fillColor=#FFD1A1;strokeColor=#B45F06;rounded=1;strokeWidth=3;align=center;verticalAlign=middle;arcSize=10;fontFamily=Helvetica;fontSize=12;fontColor=#6B2F00;rotation=0;opacity=80;" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="20" width="20" x="560" y="552" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="host" tags="level-3 Network Network.Cni Network.Cni.HostNetwork _ _.Item _.Item.NetworkUnderlayHost2 _.Kind _.Kind.Capability _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod _.Area.NetworkUnderlay" id="O8AOIrqbN8MiM61wshBk-20"> <mxCell parent="1" style="rounded=0;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;strokeWidth=1;fillColor=#e1d5e7;strokeColor=#9673a6;align=center;" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="20" width="32" x="599" y="569" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="" help="Host Networking

hostNetwork is technically neither overlay nor underlay networking. The pod shares the node’s network namespace and uses the node’s interfaces and IP addresses directly instead of receiving a normal pod network namespace.

This reduces network isolation, may bypass normal pod-level NetworkPolicy enforcement depending on the CNI, and can expose node-local services, interfaces, and ports to the workload.

Host networking should therefore normally be restricted and only allowed when explicitly required.

It goes mostly in/out the same way as underlay." tags="level-3 pri-2 Network Network.Cni Network.Cni.HostNetwork _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod _.Area.NetworkUnderlay" NetworkPolicies are applied to pods, not Kubernetes Services.
A policy selects pods using labels and controls the ingress and/or egress traffic allowed for those pods.

Enforcement happens on the pod network path and ultimately applies to traffic between pod IPs. This means the same policy applies whether traffic reaches a pod through a Service or connects directly to the pod IP.

Services may select the same pods for routing and load balancing, but they are not the enforcement point for NetworkPolicies." tags="level-2 info Network Network.Policy _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment" slug="NetpolEnforce" help.yaml.allow_app_traffic="# Pods with app=storefront: in from ingress-nginx on 8080; out only to DNS and payments-proxy:443
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
 name: storefront-allow
 namespace: shop
spec:
 podSelector:
 matchLabels:
 app: storefront
 policyTypes:
 - Ingress
 - Egress
 ingress:
 - from:
 - namespaceSelector:
 matchLabels:
 kubernetes.io/metadata.name: ingress-nginx
 podSelector:
 matchLabels:
 app.kubernetes.io/name: ingress-nginx
 ports:
 - protocol: TCP
 port: 8080
 egress:
 - to:
 - namespaceSelector:
 matchLabels:
 kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
 podSelector:
 matchLabels:
 k8s-app: kube-dns
 ports:
 - protocol: UDP
 port: 53
 - protocol: TCP
 port: 53
 - to:
 - podSelector:
 matchLabels:
 app: payments-proxy
 ports:
 - protocol: TCP
 port: 443" id="2NIop3rW37v0lhN0G3K2-27"> <mxCell parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;arcSize=10;fillColor=#DFF4FF;strokeColor=#0B6FA4;strokeWidth=3;fontColor=#0A3D5A;rotation=0;opacity=80;shadow=0;glass=0;labelBorderColor=none;textShadow=1;html=1;verticalAlign=top;" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="170" width="14" x="430" y="304" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="" tags="level-1 Network Network.Cni _ _.Line _.Line.Flow _.Item _.Item.OtherNodeNetwork _.Group _.Group.External _.Traffic _.Item.NetworkUnderlay _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod _.Area.NetworkUnderlay _.Link _.Link.NetworkUnderlayToOtherNodeNetwork" overlay="ingress,egress" id="184f-GuZHcVv3yzacIZi-3"> <mxCell edge="1" parent="1" source="O8AOIrqbN8MiM61wshBk-12" style="edgeStyle=orthogonalEdgeStyle;rounded=1;orthogonalLoop=1;jettySize=auto;html=1;exitX=1;exitY=0.5;exitDx=0;exitDy=0;jumpStyle=arc;startArrow=classic;startFill=1;entryX=0;entryY=0.485714;entryDx=0;entryDy=0;curved=0;" target="O8AOIrqbN8MiM61wshBk-1"> <mxGeometry relative="1" as="geometry"> <mxPoint x="782" y="661" as="sourcePoint" /> <mxPoint x="1071" y="661" as="targetPoint" /> </mxGeometry> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="" help="Egress

Egress policies control outbound traffic from pods using label selectors and destination IPs or CIDRs. These rules help prevent unauthorized external access.

Some CNIs support assigning dedicated egress IPs per namespace or pod, enabling traceability and firewall integration for outbound traffic control." tags="level-2 pri-3 Network Network.Egress _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="Egress" help.yaml.fixed_egress_node="# Traffic from payments-proxy to outside the cluster leaves through nodes labelled egress-gateway
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy
metadata:
 name: payments-proxy-egress
spec:
 selectors:
 - podSelector:
 matchLabels:
 io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: shop
 app: payments-proxy
 destinationCIDRs:
 - 0.0.0.0/0
 excludedCIDRs:
 - 10.0.0.0/8
 egressGateway:
 nodeSelector:
 matchLabels:
 node-role.kubernetes.io/egress-gateway: """ id="2NIop3rW37v0lhN0G3K2-84"> <mxCell parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fillColor=#FFF2A6;strokeColor=#B68A00;rounded=1;strokeWidth=3;align=center;verticalAlign=middle;arcSize=10;fontFamily=Helvetica;fontSize=12;fontColor=#5C4300;rotation=0;opacity=80;" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="20" width="20" x="977" y="394" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="" help="Traffic before filters

Traffic before reaching L7 filters (e.g., Envoy) is often encrypted with mTLS.
This makes payload inspection impossible, but metadata such as SNI, client identity, or source IP can still be used to enforce context-aware ACLs.

Use this metadata to apply fine-grained policies even when the content is opaque." tags="level-2 pri-2 Network Network.Ingress Network.Policy Network.Service Network.Service.EndpointSlice Network.Service.Port _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment" slug="PreFilter" id="gTG7mJT8VE7aOUTu5KUC-38"> <mxCell parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fillColor=#FFD1A1;strokeColor=#B45F06;rounded=1;strokeWidth=3;align=center;verticalAlign=middle;arcSize=10;fontFamily=Helvetica;fontSize=12;fontColor=#6B2F00;rotation=0;opacity=80;" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="20" width="20" x="677" y="310" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="" help="Traffic after filters

This is the raw, decrypted traffic that reaches the application after passing through L7 filters or service mesh proxies. At this point, the traffic is no longer encrypted and can be inspected or modified by sidecars or host-level tools before delivery to the application process.

Ensure that applications enforce their own validation and security controls, as traffic is now trusted and inside the protected boundary." tags="level-2 pri-3 Network Network.Ingress Network.Policy width="135" x="456" y="55" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="" help="Internal API communication

The Kubernetes API should only be accessible to internal system components, operators, and pods that explicitly require it.

Use default-deny NetworkPolicies to block access by default, and only allow specific namespaces or service accounts to communicate with the API server.
This minimizes the attack surface and enforces least privilege access." tags="level-1 pri-3 Api Api.Controllers _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="InternalApi" help.yaml.api_server_only_for_labelled_pods="# Every pod outside kube-system is denied the Kubernetes API, except pods that have the label api-access
# (a deny rule wins over any allow, so namespace policies can't open it again)
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy
metadata:
 name: api-server-only-for-labelled-pods
spec:
 endpointSelector:
 matchExpressions:
 - key: io.kubernetes.pod.namespace
 operator: NotIn
 values: ["kube-system"]
 - key: api-access
 operator: DoesNotExist
 enableDefaultDeny:
 egress: false
 egressDeny:
 - toEntities:
 - kube-apiserver" id="gTG7mJT8VE7aOUTu5KUC-47"> <mxCell parent="1" target="pqV90kVsezlGcEVYyXwn-35"> <mxGeometry relative="1" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="<font style="font-size: 18px; color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b style="">?</b></font>" help="Kubernetes objects

Everything in a cluster is an object created through the API: Deployments, Services, Secrets, NetworkPolicies, RBAC, custom resources. An object is desired state. Nothing runs just because it exists.

You typically create only a few objects yourself, with kubectl, GitOps, Helm or CI. Controllers create most of the others: a Deployment gets a ReplicaSet and the ReplicaSet gets Pods; a CronJob gets a new Job on every run and each Job gets Pods; an operator can turn one custom resource into many objects, cluster-scoped ones too.

Each of those objects is a new request to the API, made by the controller as itself. That is the feedback loop: one object leads to more, and every one of them is checked again. It is why Pod rules apply even if you only created a Deployment (the Pods are created later, by the replicaset-controller, and admission checks them then), and why a Deployment can exist while its Pods do not." tags="level-1 info Api Api.Objects _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="KubernetesObjects" id="x-6E1dSvq2MKdfss87R8-1"> <mxCell parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;arcSize=10;fillColor=#DFF4FF;strokeColor=#0B6FA4;strokeWidth=3;fontColor=#0A3D5A;rotation=0;opacity=80;shadow=0;glass=0;labelBorderColor=none;textShadow=1;html=1;" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="26" width="26" x="582" y="196" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="<font style="font-size: 18px; color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b style="">?</b></font>" help="Controllers

A controller is a program that watches objects through the API and works until the cluster matches them. This is the reconcile loop. kube-controller-manager runs the built-in ones (deployment-controller, replicaset-controller, cronjob-controller, job-controller, endpointslice-controller, ...). Operators such as cert-manager or Argo CD add their own.

A controller never writes to etcd and never creates anything directly. It sends ordinary API requests with its own identity, usually a ServiceAccount. Those requests go through authentication, RBAC and admission like any other. So a controller can only do what its RBAC allows, and admission policies (Pod Security Admission, Kyverno, Gatekeeper) still apply to what it creates. When a request is refused, nothing is created: the controller retries, and the reason shows up as events and in the status of the object it works on.

Security: controller ServiceAccounts are often powerful. Whoever can change the objects a controller acts on, or the controller itself, can make it create anything its RBAC allows." tags="level-1 info Api Api.Controllers _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="Controllers" id="x-6E1dSvq2MKdfss87R8-2"> <mxCell parent="1" style="rounded=1;whiteSpace=wrap;arcSize=10;fillColor=#DFF4FF;strokeColor=#0B6FA4;strokeWidth=3;fontColor=#0A3D5A;rotation=0;opacity=80;shadow=0;glass=0;labelBorderColor=none;textShadow=1;html=1;" </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="" tags="level-2 pri-1 Namespace Namespace.Psa _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Namespace" help="Pod Security Admission (PSA)

Pod Security Admission (PSA) enforces a baseline security level for pods in a namespace by validating pod specs at admission time (before the pod is created).

It uses namespace labels to apply standard Pod Security profiles (privileged, baseline, restricted) and can block insecure settings such as privileged containers, excessive Linux capabilities, unsafe host access, or other risky pod configurations.

PSA is an important preventive control for reducing attack surface and stopping insecure workloads before they are deployed." slug="Psa" help.yaml.enforce_baseline_warn_restricted="# Namespace labels: enforce baseline, only warn and audit on restricted
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
 name: shop
 labels:
 pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline
 pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: v1.34
 pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted
 pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn-version: v1.34
 pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted
 pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit-version: v1.34" help.log.warning_on_create="# cache-warmer.yaml: a Pod running docker.io/library/debian as root, no securityContext
$ kubectl --token="$STOLEN_TOKEN" create -f cache-warmer.yaml
Warning: would violate PodSecurity "restricted:v1.34": allowPrivilegeEscalation != false (container "cache-warmer" must set securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation=false), unrestricted capabilities (container "cache-warmer" must set securityContext.capabilities.drop=["ALL"]), runAsNonRoot != true (pod or container "cache-warmer" must set securityContext.runAsNonRoot=true), seccompProfile (pod or container "cache-warmer" must set securityContext.seccompProfile.type to "RuntimeDefault" or "Localhost")
pod/cache-warmer created" id="YWpAQDu6UTAB_IzSb4FO-20"> <mxCell parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fillColor=#FF7A7A;strokeColor=#7A1414;rounded=1;strokeWidth=3;align=center;verticalAlign=middle;arcSize=10;fontFamily=Helvetica;fontSize=12;fontColor=#5B1010;rotation=0;opacity=80;" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="20" width="20" x="965.5" y="702.5" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="" help="ResourceQuota

ResourceQuota limits the total amount of cluster resources a namespace can consume (for example CPU, memory, storage, and object counts such as pods or services).

From a security and resilience perspective, quotas help reduce denial-of-service risk inside the cluster by preventing a single namespace or team from exhausting shared resources and impacting other workloads.

ResourceQuota is primarily a governance and availability control, but it also supports multi-tenancy and safer operations by enforcing usage bounds." tags="level-2 pri-2 Namespace Namespace.Quota _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Namespace" slug="ResourceQuota" help.yaml.limit_namespace_resources="# Caps for namespace shop: total CPU/memory, number of pods, and no LoadBalancer/NodePort Services
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
 name: shop-quota
 namespace: shop
spec:
 hard:
 requests.cpu: "16"
 requests.memory: 32Gi
 limits.memory: 48Gi
 pods: "40"
 services.loadbalancers: "0"
 services.nodeports: "0"" help.shell.show_quota_usage="# Used vs. hard limit for each quota in the namespace
$ kubectl describe quota -n shop
Name: shop-quota
Namespace: shop
Resource Used Hard
-------- ---- ----
limits.memory 4352Mi 48Gi
pods 17 40
requests.cpu 3100m 16
requests.memory 2176Mi 32Gi
services.loadbalancers 0 0
services.nodeports 0 0" id="YWpAQDu6UTAB_IzSb4FO-26"> <mxCell parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fillColor=#FFD1A1;strokeColor=#B45F06;rounded=1;strokeWidth=3;align=center;verticalAlign=middle;arcSize=10;fontFamily=Helvetica;fontSize=12;fontColor=#6B2F00;rotation=0;opacity=80;" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="20" width="20" x="965.5" y="813.5" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="" help="LimitRange

LimitRange defines default and minimum/maximum resource requests and limits for containers and pods in a namespace (for example CPU and memory).

From a security and stability perspective, it helps prevent unsafe or unbounded workloads (such as containers with no limits) and improves cluster reliability by enforcing consistent resource settings.

LimitRange is mainly a stability and governance control, but it also supports safer multi-tenant operation by reducing resource abuse and misconfiguration." tags="level-2 pri-2 Namespace Namespace.Quota _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Namespace" slug="LimitRange" help.yaml.default_container_limits="# Containers without requests/limits get these defaults; more than 2Gi memory is rejected
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
 name: shop-defaults
 namespace: shop
spec:
 limits:
 - type: Container
 defaultRequest:
 cpu: 100m
 memory: 128Mi
 default:
 memory: 256Mi
 max:
 memory: 2Gi" help.shell.show_limit_defaults="# Defaults applied to containers that set no requests/limits
$ kubectl describe limitrange -n shop
Name: shop-defaults
Namespace: shop
Type Resource Min Max Default Request Default Limit Max Limit/Request Ratio
---- -------- --- --- --------------- ------------- -----------------------
Container memory - 2Gi 128Mi 256Mi -
Container cpu - - 100m - -" id="YWpAQDu6UTAB_IzSb4FO-27"> <mxCell parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fillColor=#FFD1A1;strokeColor=#B45F06;rounded=1;strokeWidth=3;align=center;verticalAlign=middle;arcSize=10;fontFamily=Helvetica;fontSize=12;fontColor=#6B2F00;rotation=0;opacity=80;" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="20" width="20" x="965.5" y="851.5" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="" help="Default ServiceAccount

Every namespace has a default ServiceAccount (unless automountServiceAccountToken=false), and pods use it automatically unless another ServiceAccount is explicitly configured. From a security perspective, this matters because unintended API access can be granted if the default account has permissions or if service account tokens are auto-mounted unnecessarily." tags="level-2 pri-3 Namespace Namespace.DefaultSa _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Namespace" slug="DefaultSa" help.yaml.disable_token_automount="# Pods using the default ServiceAccount get no API token mounted
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
 name: default
 namespace: shop
automountServiceAccountToken: false" id="YWpAQDu6UTAB_IzSb4FO-29"> <mxCell parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fillColor=#FFF2A6;strokeColor=#B68A00;rounded=1;strokeWidth=3;align=center;verticalAlign=middle;arcSize=10;fontFamily=Helvetica;fontSize=12;fontColor=#5C4300;rotation=0;opacity=80;" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="20" width="20" x="965.5" y="923.5" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="" tags="level-2 pri-1 Namespace Network Network.Policy _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Namespace" slug="NsDefaultDeny" help.yaml.deny_all_traffic="# Selects every pod in shop; no rules means no traffic in or out
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
 name: default-deny
 namespace: shop
spec:
 podSelector: {}
 policyTypes:
 - Ingress
 - Egress" help="Default deny NetworkPolicy

A namespace starts with no NetworkPolicy, and then every pod accepts traffic from everywhere in the cluster and can send traffic anywhere. A default-deny policy per namespace (an empty podSelector with policyTypes Ingress and Egress) flips that: only traffic that another policy allows gets through.

Add explicit allows on top: DNS to kube-dns, traffic from the ingress controller, and the few services each app needs. Without this, one compromised pod can reach every other pod and service in the cluster." id="ns-suggest-0-pri"> <mxCell parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;rounded=1;strokeWidth=3;align=center;verticalAlign=middle;arcSize=10;fontFamily=Helvetica;fontSize=12;rotation=0;opacity=80;fillColor=#FF7A7A;strokeColor=#7A1414;fontColor=#5B1010;" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="20" width="20" x="965.5" y="739.5" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="" tags="level-2 pri-1 Namespace Api Api.Rbac Api.Rbac.Binding _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Namespace" slug="NsTeamAccess" help.yaml.team_edit_access="# Group shop-developers gets the built-in edit role, only in namespace shop
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
 name: shop-developers-edit
 namespace: shop
subjects:
 - kind: Group
 name: shop-developers
 apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
 apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
 kind: ClusterRole
 name: edit" help.shell.check_team_permissions="# edit can exec into pods and add debug containers, but not change RBAC
$ kubectl auth can-i create rolebindings -n shop --as=jberg@fjordmart.example --as-group=shop-developers
no
$ kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec -n shop --as=jberg@fjordmart.example --as-group=shop-developers
yes
$ kubectl auth can-i patch pods/ephemeralcontainers -n shop --as=jberg@fjordmart.example --as-group=shop-developers
yes" help="Team access with RoleBindings

Give teams access to their namespace with a RoleBinding to a Role or to a built-in ClusterRole such as edit or view. A RoleBinding only grants rights inside its own namespace, even when it points to a ClusterRole.

Avoid ClusterRoleBindings for app teams, avoid giving them the admin role unless they should manage RBAC themselves, and never bind to the default ServiceAccount. Review who can create RoleBindings: that right lets someone grant themselves more." id="ns-suggest-1-pri"> <mxCell parent="1" style="ellipse;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;rounded=1;strokeWidth=3;align=center;verticalAlign=middle;arcSize=10;fontFamily=Helvetica;fontSize=12;rotation=0;opacity=80;fillColor=#FF7A7A;strokeColor=#7A1414;fontColor=#5B1010;" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="20" width="20" x="965.5" y="776.5" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </UserObject> <UserObject label="" tags="level-2 pri-3 Namespace _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Namespace" slug="NsLabels" help="Namespace labels

Labels on the namespace drive a lot of security: Pod Security Admission levels (pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce), which admission policies apply, mesh injection, NetworkPolicy namespaceSelectors and cost or team ownership.

Treat them as configuration: set them from GitOps, and restrict who can change them, since changing a label can switch a control off." id="ns-suggest-9-pri"> <mxCell parent="1" <UserObject label="<font style="font-size: 18px; color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b style="">?</b></font>" help="Kernel Activity (what runtime instrumentation sees)

A container process is a normal host process: every exec, file open and connection goes through the host kernel. Runtime security tools (Tetragon, Falco) attach eBPF programs to kernel hooks and read the activity there, without an agent in the pod and regardless of what the image contains.
Each event carries the task's cgroup ID and namespace IDs, which the tool maps to container, Pod, namespace and workload via the container runtime (CRI) and the Kubernetes API.

<b>Sources</b>
- process-exec: execve/execveat, tracepoint sched_process_exec, LSM hook bprm_check_security. Binary, arguments, UID/GID, capabilities, cwd.
- process-tree: built by the tool from fork (wake_up_new_task, sched_process_fork) and exit (acct_process, sched_process_exit). Parent chain back to containerd-shim/runc, so a shell spawned by a web server stands out.
- syscalls: raw tracepoints sys_enter/sys_exit (Falco's base source), or kprobes on single syscalls such as __x64_sys_setuid or __x64_sys_ptrace (Tetragon TracingPolicy).
- network: tcp_connect, inet_csk_accept, tcp_sendmsg, udp_sendmsg, tcp_close, tracepoint sock:inet_sock_set_state. 5-tuple per process, not only per pod.
- socket: security_socket_create, security_socket_bind, security_socket_listen, security_socket_connect. Unexpected listeners, raw and packet sockets.
- file-access: security_file_open, security_file_permission, security_mmap_file, fd_install. Reads of /etc/shadow, ServiceAccount tokens, host paths.
- file-change: security_path_unlink, security_path_rename, security_path_chmod, security_path_truncate, security_inode_setattr. Dropped binaries, changed configs.

<b>Hook types</b>
- Tracepoints are a stable kernel interface.
- Kprobes/fentry can hook any kernel function, but names and arguments change between kernel versions.
- LSM BPF hooks (CONFIG_BPF_LSM) and functions that allow error injection can also deny: Tetragon can override the return value or send SIGKILL in the kernel, before the action completes.

Falco is syscall-based: file and network activity are read from the syscalls. Tetragon hooks the kernel functions behind them, which avoids TOCTOU gaps in syscall arguments.

<b>Limits</b>
- Kata, gVisor and VMs run the workload on their own guest kernel or sandbox: the host's eBPF sees the sandbox, not the process inside.
- Hooking every syscall or file read costs CPU. Filter in the kernel (Tetragon selectors, Falco's event set) and send on only what matters.
- Events stay on the node; forward them to a central system to correlate and keep them." tags="level-3 info Node Node.RuntimeSecurity _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod _.Area.Container _.Area.Process _.Area.KernelActivity" slug="KernelActivity" help.json.process_exec_event="# Tetragon process_exec event (trimmed): binary started from /tmp in pod shop/cache-warmer

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="font-size: 18px; color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b style="">?</b></font>" help="What is this and how to use..
This is a diagram made to better understand and get an overview of kubernetes security.

It's not complete (but you are welcome to submitt a PR/issue), nor is it perfect, it is biased and it might not be for you.

It might however help you to discuss kubernetes in a security-context with your team, or just to get a better understanding yourself.

The drawing is most likely an overkill. It is not ment as a "solution" or design.
It's also quite busy, with a ton of elements. It's not ment to "explain" everything, but something you can sit down with and browse around and maybe learn something new.

Also, it is on-prem... For non on-prem, it might not be that relevant." tags="info" slug="Info"/>

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="font-size: 18px; color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b style="">?</b></font>" help="What is an "operator"

Operators in Kubernetes extend the control plane by automating the management of complex applications or infrastructure using custom resources and controllers.

For example, a system operator can create defaults like Namespaces, or manage external resources through custom objects like a "Tofu" resource controlling infrastructure outside the cluster.

Kubernetes can serve as a generic orchestration engine—beyond just container workloads." tags="level-2 info CustomOperator _ _.Area _.Area.CustomOperator" slug="Operator"/>
g.data-help:
What is an "operator"
Operators in Kubernetes extend the control plane by automating the management of complex applications or infrastructure using custom resources and controllers.
For example, a system operator can create defaults like Namespaces, or manage external resources through custom objects like a "Tofu" resource controlling infrastructure outside the cluster.
Kubernetes can serve as a generic orchestration engine—beyond just container workloads.

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="font-size: 18px; color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b style="">?</b></font>" help="ResourceQuota vs LimitRange

ResourceQuota limits the total resources and object counts a namespace can use, which helps prevent one team/app from exhausting shared cluster capacity (for example creating too many pods/services or consuming too much CPU, memory, or storage).

LimitRange sets default and min/max resource requests and limits for pods/containers in that namespace, which helps prevent unsafe or unstable workloads (for example containers with no memory limit, or requests/limits that are far too high or too low)." tags="level-2 info Namespace Namespace.Quota _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Namespace" slug="QuotaVsLimits"/>
g.data-help:
ResourceQuota vs LimitRange
ResourceQuota limits the total resources and object counts a namespace can use, which helps prevent one team/app from exhausting shared cluster capacity (for example creating too many pods/services or consuming too much CPU, memory, or storage).
LimitRange sets default and min/max resource requests and limits for pods/containers in that namespace, which helps prevent unsafe or unstable workloads (for example containers with no memory limit, or requests/limits that are far too high or too low).

g.content:
<UserObject label="" tags="level-1 pri-1 _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod _.Area.Container" help="The Container Process

Containerized workloads are secured through PodSecurityContext/SecurityContext, Pod Security Standards (PSA), namespace isolation, and runtime enforcement.
Tools like Falco (eBPF) monitor behavior, while KubeArmor enforces policies.
Enterprise options include Sysdig Secure, Tetragon, Prisma Cloud, and the open-source NeuVector.

Syscalls are restricted by default; escapes often rely on misconfigurations such as excessive Linux capabilities, unfiltered syscalls, insecure mounts, or relaxed namespace settings.

Linux namespaces isolate PIDs, networking, and other kernel features; cgroups control CPU/memory and can freeze containers for forensics.

Runtime policies like runAsNonRoot or fixed UID/GID can be set at the container/pod level or baked into the image." slug="ContainerProcess"/>
g.data-help:
The Container Process
Containerized workloads are secured through PodSecurityContext/SecurityContext, Pod Security Standards (PSA), namespace isolation, and runtime enforcement. Tools like Falco (eBPF) monitor behavior, while KubeArmor enforces policies. Enterprise options include Sysdig Secure, Tetragon, Prisma Cloud, and the open-source NeuVector.
Syscalls are restricted by default; escapes often rely on misconfigurations such as excessive Linux capabilities, unfiltered syscalls, insecure mounts, or relaxed namespace settings.
Linux namespaces isolate PIDs, networking, and other kernel features; cgroups control CPU/memory and can freeze containers for forensics.
Runtime policies like runAsNonRoot or fixed UID/GID can be set at the container/pod level or baked into the image.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 122, 122), rgb(198, 84, 84)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(122, 20, 20), rgb(255, 183, 183));

g.content:
<UserObject label="" tags="level-2 pri-1 Network Network.Policy _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" help="Network Control

Network policies can enforce L3/L4 restrictions using eBPF or iptables, while L7 policies are enforced via proxies (e.g., Envoy).

Some CNIs support admin-level policies that cannot be overridden by namespace users, enabling enforcement of cluster-wide or organizational security standards." slug="NetworkControl" help.yaml.cluster_wide_policies="# Cilium, cluster-wide: DNS visibility for every pod, and no pod may reach 10.20.0.0/16 (deny wins over any allow)
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy
metadata:
 name: intercept-all-dns
spec:
 endpointSelector:
 matchExpressions:
 - key: io.kubernetes.pod.namespace
 operator: NotIn
 values:
 - kube-system
 enableDefaultDeny:
 egress: false
 ingress: false
 egress:
 - toEndpoints:
 - matchLabels:
 io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: kube-system
 k8s-app: kube-dns
 toPorts:
 - ports:
 - port: "53"
 protocol: TCP
 - port: "53"
 protocol: UDP
 rules:
 dns:
 - matchPattern: "*"
---
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy
metadata:
 name: deny-pods-to-corp-lan
spec:
 endpointSelector:
 matchExpressions:
 - key: io.kubernetes.pod.namespace
 operator: NotIn
 values:
 - kube-system
 - monitoring
 enableDefaultDeny:
 egress: false
 egressDeny:
 - toCIDRSet:
 - cidr: 10.20.0.0/16" help.yaml.admin_and_baseline_tiers="# Upstream ClusterNetworkPolicy (network-policy-api v1alpha2); Baseline tier = defaults that namespace policies can override
apiVersion: policy.networking.k8s.io/v1alpha2
kind: ClusterNetworkPolicy
metadata:
 name: cluster-baseline
spec:
 tier: Baseline
 priority: 100
 subject:
 namespaces:
 matchLabels:
 kubernetes.io/metadata.name: shop
 ingress:
 - name: deny-from-other-namespaces
 action: Deny
 from:
 - namespaces:
 matchExpressions:
 - key: kubernetes.io/metadata.name
 operator: NotIn
 values: ["shop", "ingress-nginx", "monitoring"]
 egress:
 - name: deny-corp-lan
 action: Deny
 to:
 - networks: ["10.20.0.0/16"]"/>
g.data-help:
Network Control
Network policies can enforce L3/L4 restrictions using eBPF or iptables, while L7 policies are enforced via proxies (e.g., Envoy).
Some CNIs support admin-level policies that cannot be overridden by namespace users, enabling enforcement of cluster-wide or organizational security standards.

g.data-help.yaml.admin_and_baseline_tiers: # Upstream ClusterNetworkPolicy (network-policy-api v1alpha2); Baseline tier = defaults that namespace policies can override apiVersion: policy.networking.k8s.io/v1alpha2 kind: ClusterNetworkPolicy metadata: name: cluster-baseline spec: tier: Baseline priority: 100 subject: namespaces: matchLabels: kubernetes.io/metadata.name: shop ingress: - name: deny-from-other-namespaces action: Deny from: - namespaces: matchExpressions: - key: kubernetes.io/metadata.name operator: NotIn values: ["shop", "ingress-nginx", "monitoring"] egress: - name: deny-corp-lan action: Deny to: - networks: ["10.20.0.0/16"]

g.content:
<UserObject label="" tags="level-2 pri-1 Network Network.Ingress Ingress Ingress.Controller _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" help="Ingress

Kubernetes Ingress resources configure an ingress controller (e.g., NGINX, HAProxy) to handle inbound traffic. Controllers support annotations for TLS settings, authentication, WAF (e.g., ModSecurity), and other security features.

Routing is typically based on SNI (FQDN) and HTTP-layer data such as path, method, or headers. Secure configuration of the ingress controller is critical, including rate limiting, header validation, and TLS hardening.

For new designs, prefer Gateway API where possible. Gateway API provides a more structured and extensible model for routing, policy attachment, and role separation, and is the main direction of ongoing ecosystem development." slug="Ingress" help.yaml.tls_ingress="# HTTPS for shop.fjordmart.example; TLS ends at the ingress controller with Secret shop-fjordmart-tls
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
 name: storefront
 namespace: shop
spec:
 ingressClassName: nginx
 tls:
 - hosts:
 - shop.fjordmart.example
 secretName: shop-fjordmart-tls
 rules:
 - host: shop.fjordmart.example
 http:
 paths:
 - path: /
 pathType: Prefix
 backend:
 service:
 name: storefront
 port:
 name: http"/>
g.data-tags: level-2 pri-1 Network Network.Ingress Ingress Ingress.Controller _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster
g.data-help:
Ingress
Kubernetes Ingress resources configure an ingress controller (e.g., NGINX, HAProxy) to handle inbound traffic. Controllers support annotations for TLS settings, authentication, WAF (e.g., ModSecurity), and other security features.
Routing is typically based on SNI (FQDN) and HTTP-layer data such as path, method, or headers. Secure configuration of the ingress controller is critical, including rate limiting, header validation, and TLS hardening.
For new designs, prefer Gateway API where possible. Gateway API provides a more structured and extensible model for routing, policy attachment, and role separation, and is the main direction of ongoing ecosystem development.
g.data-help.yaml.tls_ingress: # HTTPS for shop.fjordmart.example; TLS ends at the ingress controller with Secret shop-fjordmart-tls apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Ingress metadata: name: storefront namespace: shop spec: ingressClassName: nginx tls: - hosts: - shop.fjordmart.example secretName: shop-fjordmart-tls rules: - host: shop.fjordmart.example http: paths: - path: / pathType: Prefix backend: service: name: storefront port: name: http

g.content:
<UserObject label="" tags="pri-1 Api _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" help="Kubernetes API

The Kubernetes API is the primary control plane entry point and must be tightly secured.
All access passes through two stages: authentication and authorization.

API call is first ratelimited using <a target=_blank href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/cluster-administration/flow-control/">priority and fairness</a>.

Authentication verifies the caller (client certificates, bearer tokens, OIDC, or webhook tokens).
Anonymous requests are allowed by default (should be disabled in production).

Authorization decides if the authenticated identity may act. Kubernetes supports:
- RBAC (Role-Based Access Control): recommended and widely adopted.
- Webhook Authorization: delegate decisions to an external policy engine.
- ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control): legacy and strongly discouraged; keep only for backward compatibility and plan to migrate off it.

RBAC grants fine-grained verbs (GET, CREATE, etc.) over resources and API groups via roles/bindings.
ABAC uses JSON policy files but is harder to audit and operate at scale.

Enable API server audit logging and ship logs to a remote backend for monitoring and incident response." slug="KubeApi" help.yaml.oidc_and_anonymous_config="# kube-apiserver --authentication-config=/etc/kubernetes/authentication-config.yaml
# Users log in with OIDC (Keycloak); anonymous requests only reach the health endpoints
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: AuthenticationConfiguration
jwt:
 - issuer:
 url: https://sso.fjordmart.example/realms/fjordmart
 audiences:
 - kubernetes
 claimMappings:
 username:
 claim: email
 prefix: ""
 groups:
 claim: groups
 prefix: ""
 userValidationRules:
 - expression: "!user.username.startsWith('system:')"
 message: 'username cannot use the reserved system: prefix'
 - expression: "user.groups.all(g, !g.startsWith('system:'))"
 message: 'groups cannot use the reserved system: prefix'
anonymous:
 enabled: true
 conditions:
 - path: /livez
 - path: /readyz
 - path: /healthz" help.json.anonymous_request_denied="# Anonymous request to the API: only /livez, /readyz and /healthz are open
$ curl -sk https://k8s-prod.fjordmart.example:6443/api
{
 "kind": "Status",
 "apiVersion": "v1",
 "metadata": {},
 "status": "Failure",
 "message": "Unauthorized",
 "reason": "Unauthorized",
 "code": 401
}"/>
g.data-help: Kubernetes API The Kubernetes API is the primary control plane entry point and must be tightly secured. All access passes through two stages: authentication and authorization. API call is first ratelimited using priority and fairness. Authentication verifies the caller (client certificates, bearer tokens, OIDC, or webhook tokens). Anonymous requests are allowed by default (should be disabled in production). Authorization decides if the authenticated identity may act. Kubernetes supports: - RBAC (Role-Based Access Control): recommended and widely adopted. - Webhook Authorization: delegate decisions to an external policy engine. - ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control): legacy and strongly discouraged; keep only for backward compatibility and plan to migrate off it. RBAC grants fine-grained verbs (GET, CREATE, etc.) over resources and API groups via roles/bindings. ABAC uses JSON policy files but is harder to audit and operate at scale. Enable API server audit logging and ship logs to a remote backend for monitoring and incident response.
g.data-help.yaml.oidc_and_anonymous_config: # kube-apiserver --authentication-config=/etc/kubernetes/authentication-config.yaml # Users log in with OIDC (Keycloak); anonymous requests only reach the health endpoints apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1 kind: AuthenticationConfiguration jwt: - issuer: url: https://sso.fjordmart.example/realms/fjordmart audiences: - kubernetes claimMappings: username: claim: email prefix: "" groups: claim: groups prefix: "" userValidationRules: - expression: "!user.username.startsWith('system:')" message: 'username cannot use the reserved system: prefix' - expression: "user.groups.all(g, !g.startsWith('system:'))" message: 'groups cannot use the reserved system: prefix' anonymous: enabled: true conditions: - path: /livez - path: /readyz - path: /healthz
g.data-help.json.anonymous_request_denied: # Anonymous request to the API: only /livez, /readyz and /healthz are open $ curl -sk https://k8s-prod.fjordmart.example:6443/api { "kind": "Status", "apiVersion": "v1", "metadata": {}, "status": "Failure", "message": "Unauthorized", "reason": "Unauthorized", "code": 401 }

g.content:
<UserObject label="" tags="level-3 pri-1 Api Api.Rbac _ _.Area _.Area.Rbac" help="RBAC

<a target=_blank href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/rbac/">RBAC</a> authorizes a request by matching the caller (User/Group/ServiceAccount) to bindings, which reference roles containing rules (verbs/resources/apiGroups).

<b>Role and RoleBindings</b>
* Role: used by RoleBinding (same namespace)
* ClusterRole (cluster-scoped): used by ClusterRoleBinding (cluster-wide) or RoleBinding (namespaced)
* RoleBinding (namespaced) can reference Role or ClusterRole
* ClusterRoleBinding (cluster-scoped) can reference only ClusterRole

<b><a target=_blank href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/rbac/#referring-to-subjects">Subjects</a></b>
* User (global): not a Kubernetes resource; comes from authentication (cert/OIDC/webhook)
* Group (global): not a resource; assigned by the identity provider
* ServiceAccount (namespaced resource): must include namespace in bindings (also in ClusterRoleBinding). RoleBindings can only use ServiceAccounts from their own namespace

Rules specify <code>apiGroups</code>, <code>resources</code>, <code>resourceNames</code> (optional), and <code>verbs</code> (e.g., get,list,watch,create,update,patch,delete).
Non-resource URLs use <code>nonResourceURLs</code>.

<b>Warnings</b>
* Wildcards: avoid <code>"*"</code> for verbs/resources/apiGroups unless truly needed
* <code>escalate</code> verb (on roles/clusterroles): allows creating/updating roles with permissions beyond your own
* <code>bind</code> verb (on clusterroles): allows binding clusterroles you don't otherwise “own”
* <code>impersonate</code> verb: restrict tightly; lets callers act as other users/groups/SAs (<a target=_blank href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/authentication/#user-impersonation">Impersonation docs</a>)
* Node/proxy (e.g. nodes/proxy, nodes/*, services/proxy, pods/proxy): Permissions that enable proxying via the API server can look harmless for monitoring, but effectively grant access to node/kubelet (and other proxied) HTTP endpoints. Treat as high-risk: avoid wildcards, scope tightly (resourceNames/namespaces), and only grant if you fully understand the blast radius and the exact endpoints the client can reach. This includes the GET verb!" slug="Rbac" help.yaml.over_privileged_role="# Meant for reading config, but "create pods" lets the ServiceAccount start any pod in shop
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
 name: storefront
 namespace: shop
rules:
 - apiGroups: [""]
 resources: ["configmaps"]
 verbs: ["get", "list"]
 - apiGroups: [""]
 resources: ["pods"]
 verbs: ["create"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
 name: storefront
 namespace: shop
subjects:
 - kind: ServiceAccount
 name: storefront
 namespace: shop
roleRef:
 apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
 kind: Role
 name: storefront" help.shell.check_serviceaccount_permissions="# What the storefront ServiceAccount is allowed to do
$ kubectl auth can-i create pods -n shop --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:storefront
yes
$ kubectl auth can-i create pods -n kube-system --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:storefront
no
$ kubectl auth can-i --list -n shop --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:storefront | head -6
Resources Non-Resource URLs Resource Names Verbs
pods [] [] [create]
selfsubjectreviews.authentication.k8s.io [] [] [create]
selfsubjectaccessreviews.authorization.k8s.io [] [] [create]
selfsubjectrulesreviews.authorization.k8s.io [] [] [create]
configmaps [] [] [get list]"/>
g.data-help: RBAC RBAC authorizes a request by matching the caller (User/Group/ServiceAccount) to bindings, which reference roles containing rules (verbs/resources/apiGroups). Role and RoleBindings * Role: used by RoleBinding (same namespace) * ClusterRole (cluster-scoped): used by ClusterRoleBinding (cluster-wide) or RoleBinding (namespaced) * RoleBinding (namespaced) can reference Role or ClusterRole * ClusterRoleBinding (cluster-scoped) can reference only ClusterRole Subjects * User (global): not a Kubernetes resource; comes from authentication (cert/OIDC/webhook) * Group (global): not a resource; assigned by the identity provider * ServiceAccount (namespaced resource): must include namespace in bindings (also in ClusterRoleBinding). RoleBindings can only use ServiceAccounts from their own namespace Rules specify apiGroups, resources, resourceNames (optional), and verbs (e.g., get,list,watch,create,update,patch,delete). Non-resource URLs use nonResourceURLs. Warnings * Wildcards: avoid "*" for verbs/resources/apiGroups unless truly needed * escalate verb (on roles/clusterroles): allows creating/updating roles with permissions beyond your own * bind verb (on clusterroles): allows binding clusterroles you don't otherwise “own” * impersonate verb: restrict tightly; lets callers act as other users/groups/SAs (Impersonation docs) * Node/proxy (e.g. nodes/proxy, nodes/*, services/proxy, pods/proxy): Permissions that enable proxying via the API server can look harmless for monitoring, but effectively grant access to node/kubelet (and other proxied) HTTP endpoints. Treat as high-risk: avoid wildcards, scope tightly (resourceNames/namespaces), and only grant if you fully understand the blast radius and the exact endpoints the client can reach. This includes the GET verb!
g.data-help.yaml.over_privileged_role: # Meant for reading config, but "create pods" lets the ServiceAccount start any pod in shop apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: Role metadata: name: storefront namespace: shop rules: - apiGroups: [""] resources: ["configmaps"] verbs: ["get", "list"] - apiGroups: [""] resources: ["pods"] verbs: ["create"] --- apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: RoleBinding metadata: name: storefront namespace: shop subjects: - kind: ServiceAccount name: storefront namespace: shop roleRef: apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io kind: Role name: storefront
g.data-help.shell.check_serviceaccount_per: # What the storefront ServiceAccount is allowed to do $ kubectl auth can-i create pods -n shop --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:storefront yes $ kubectl auth can-i create pods -n kube-system --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:storefront no $ kubectl auth can-i --list -n shop --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:storefront | head -6 Resources Non-Resource URLs Resource Names Verbs pods [] [] [create] selfsubjectreviews.authentication.k8s.io [] [] [create] selfsubjectaccessreviews.authorization.k8s.io [] [] [create] selfsubjectrulesreviews.authorization.k8s.io [] [] [create] configmaps [] [] [get list]

g.content:
<UserObject label="" tags="pri-1 Namespace _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" help="Namespaces

Namespaces are logical boundaries used to apply security controls such as network policies, RBAC, and runtime restrictions.

While not a security mechanism by themselves, they enable isolation between workloads and enforce separation of concerns.

Many controls are applied per namespace, including Pod Security Admission (PSA) profiles, ResourceQuota, LimitRange, NetworkPolicy, and the default ServiceAccount used by pods unless explicitly overridden.

This makes namespaces important for multi-tenancy, workload isolation, and applying different security baselines across teams or environments.

Do not confuse Kubernetes namespaces with Linux process namespaces inside containers." slug="Namespace"/>
g.data-help:
Namespaces
Namespaces are logical boundaries used to apply security controls such as network policies, RBAC, and runtime restrictions.
While not a security mechanism by themselves, they enable isolation between workloads and enforce separation of concerns.
Many controls are applied per namespace, including Pod Security Admission (PSA) profiles, ResourceQuota, LimitRange, NetworkPolicy, and the default ServiceAccount used by pods unless explicitly overridden.
This makes namespaces important for multi-tenancy, workload isolation, and applying different security baselines across teams or environments.
Do not confuse Kubernetes namespaces with Linux process namespaces inside containers.

<UserObject label="" tags="level-1 pri-1 SupplyChain SupplyChain.Registry" help="Image Repository

Container images should be scanned for vulnerabilities before being stored in or pulled from the image repository.

Use tools that enforce image admission policies, signature verification, and vulnerability thresholds to block untrusted or outdated images." slug="ImageRepo"/>
g.data-help:
Image Repository
Container images should be scanned for vulnerabilities before being stored in or pulled from the image repository.
Use tools that enforce image admission policies, signature verification, and vulnerability thresholds to block untrusted or outdated images.
