g.content:
<UserObject label="" tags="level-3 pri-1 Ingress Ingress.GatewayApi Ingress.GatewayApi.Gateway _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" help="Gateway

Kubernetes Gateway resources are part of Gateway API and define how traffic enters the cluster, including listeners (ports, protocols, hostnames) and TLS configuration (for example certificate references).

A Gateway is attached to a GatewayClass (implementation/controller) and is typically used together with Route resources (such as HTTPRoute or TCPRoute) that define traffic matching and forwarding behavior.

From a security perspective, Gateway is a key enforcement point for exposed services: it defines which protocols and hostnames are accepted, where TLS is terminated, and which certificates are used. Additional security controls are typically attached through policy resources (for example authentication, authorization, rate limiting, and WAF-related controls), while routes define how traffic is forwarded.

Gateway API separates infrastructure ownership (GatewayClass / Gateway) from application routing (*Route) and policy attachment (*Policy), making it a more structured and extensible model for secure, modern traffic management.
" slug="Gateway" help.yaml.https_listener="# HTTPS listener for shop.fjordmart.example; only routes from namespace shop may attach
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
 name: public
 namespace: gateway-system
spec:
 gatewayClassName: kgateway
 listeners:
 - name: shop-https
 protocol: HTTPS
 port: 443
 hostname: shop.fjordmart.example
 tls:
 mode: Terminate
 certificateRefs:
 - kind: Secret
 name: shop-fjordmart-tls
 namespace: shop
 allowedRoutes:
 namespaces:
 from: Selector
 selector:
 matchLabels:
 kubernetes.io/metadata.name: shop" help.yaml.route_to_service="# All paths on shop.fjordmart.example go to Service storefront port 80
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
 name: storefront
 namespace: shop
spec:
 parentRefs:
 - name: public
 namespace: gateway-system
 sectionName: shop-https
 hostnames:
 - shop.fjordmart.example
 rules:
 - matches:
 - path:
 type: PathPrefix
 value: /
 backendRefs:
 - name: storefront
 port: 80"/>
g.data-help:
Gateway
Kubernetes Gateway resources are part of Gateway API and define how traffic enters the cluster, including listeners (ports, protocols, hostnames) and TLS configuration (for example certificate references).
A Gateway is attached to a GatewayClass (implementation/controller) and is typically used together with Route resources (such as HTTPRoute or TCPRoute) that define traffic matching and forwarding behavior.
From a security perspective, Gateway is a key enforcement point for exposed services: it defines which protocols and hostnames are accepted, where TLS is terminated, and which certificates are used. Additional security controls are typically attached through policy resources (for example authentication, authorization, rate limiting, and WAF-related controls), while routes define how traffic is forwarded.
Gateway API separates infrastructure ownership (GatewayClass / Gateway) from application routing (*Route) and policy attachment (*Policy), making it a more structured and extensible model for secure, modern traffic management.
g.data-help.yaml.https_listener: # HTTPS listener for shop.fjordmart.example; only routes from namespace shop may attach apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Gateway metadata: name: public namespace: gateway-system spec: gatewayClassName: kgateway listeners: - name: shop-https protocol: HTTPS port: 443 hostname: shop.fjordmart.example tls: mode: Terminate certificateRefs: - kind: Secret name: shop-fjordmart-tls namespace: shop allowedRoutes: namespaces: from: Selector selector: matchLabels: kubernetes.io/metadata.name: shop
g.data-help.yaml.route_to_service: # All paths on shop.fjordmart.example go to Service storefront port 80 apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: HTTPRoute metadata: name: storefront namespace: shop spec: parentRefs: - name: public namespace: gateway-system sectionName: shop-https hostnames: - shop.fjordmart.example rules: - matches: - path: type: PathPrefix value: / backendRefs: - name: storefront port: 80

g.content:
<UserObject label="" tags="level-3 pri-1 Ingress Ingress.GatewayApi Ingress.GatewayApi.Gateway _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" help="GatewayClass

GatewayClass selects which Gateway API controller implementation manages a Gateway (for example Envoy Gateway, Kong, Traefik, NGINX Gateway Fabric, or a cloud-managed implementation).

This is a key trust boundary: controllers differ in supported spec versions, conformance level, feature maturity, and security/policy behavior. Gateway API conformance helps validate what is actually implemented." slug="GatewayClass" help.yaml.select_controller="# Gateways with gatewayClassName kgateway are run by the kgateway controller
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: GatewayClass
metadata:
 name: kgateway
spec:
 controllerName: kgateway.dev/kgateway"/>
g.data-help:
GatewayClass
GatewayClass selects which Gateway API controller implementation manages a Gateway (for example Envoy Gateway, Kong, Traefik, NGINX Gateway Fabric, or a cloud-managed implementation).
This is a key trust boundary: controllers differ in supported spec versions, conformance level, feature maturity, and security/policy behavior. Gateway API conformance helps validate what is actually implemented.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Service Portal

Non-admin users should request cluster resources through a service portal instead of direct kubectl access. This portal can generate GitOps-compatible manifests and apply policy-based validation before committing to Git.

It must be separate from administrative tools and enforce access control and input validation." tags="level-2 pri-2 Access Access.Portal" slug="ServicePortal"/>
g.data-help:
Service Portal
Non-admin users should request cluster resources through a service portal instead of direct kubectl access. This portal can generate GitOps-compatible manifests and apply policy-based validation before committing to Git.
It must be separate from administrative tools and enforce access control and input validation.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Container image

Container runtimes can be configured to only allow signed images using tools like sigstore/cosign.
Admission controllers such as Kyverno can enforce signature verification and additional build metadata (e.g., SLSA provenance).

Images should also be scanned for vulnerabilities before deployment and flagged or blocked based on severity thresholds." tags="level-1 pri-2 SupplyChain SupplyChain.Registry _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod _.Area.Container" slug="Image" help.shell.verify_signature="# Verify the image signature with the key in Vault; an unsigned image fails
$ cosign verify --key hashivault://shop-images registry.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront@sha256:3c9e1f7a5b2d48e06a1c9f3b7d5e2a084f6c1b9d3e7a5f20c8b4d6e1a9f3c7b2 > /dev/null

Verification for registry.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront@sha256:3c9e1f7a5b2d48e06a1c9f3b7d5e2a084f6c1b9d3e7a5f20c8b4d6e1a9f3c7b2 --
The following checks were performed on each of these signatures:
 - The cosign claims were validated
 - Existence of the claims in the transparency log was verified offline
 - The signatures were verified against the specified public key
$ cosign verify --key hashivault://shop-images docker.io/library/debian@sha256:9d4bf569e737266d93655e630c601e8810000116f0681e70f489c347717bd590
Error: no signatures found
error during command execution: no signatures found"/>
g.data-help:
Container image
Container runtimes can be configured to only allow signed images using tools like sigstore/cosign. Admission controllers such as Kyverno can enforce signature verification and additional build metadata (e.g., SLSA provenance).
Images should also be scanned for vulnerabilities before deployment and flagged or blocked based on severity thresholds.
g.data-help.shell.verify_signature:
# Verify the image signature with the key in Vault; an unsigned image fails $ cosign verify --key hashivault://shop-images registry.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront@sha256:3c9e1f7a5b2d48e06a1c9f3b7d5e2a084f6c1b9d3e7a5f20c8b4d6e1a9f3c7b2 > /dev/null
Verification for registry.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront@sha256:3c9e1f7a5b2d48e06a1c9f3b7d5e2a084f6c1b9d3e7a5f20c8b4d6e1a9f3c7b2 -- The following checks were performed on each of these signatures: - The cosign claims were validated - Existence of the claims in the transparency log was verified offline - The signatures were verified against the specified public key $ cosign verify --key hashivault://shop-images docker.io/library/debian@sha256:9d4bf569e737266d93655e630c601e8810000116f0681e70f489c347717bd590 Error: no signatures found error during command execution: no signatures found

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Mounted volumes and env-vars

External data is often injected into pods via environment variables or projected volumes.
These are typically read-only and can include ConfigMaps, Secrets, or dynamic runtime values like the pod IP or namespace.

When a pod needs to interact with the Kubernetes API, a service account token is automatically mounted as a projected volume. Ensure proper RBAC scoping for the associated service account to avoid privilege escalation." tags="level-2 pri-2 Workload Workload.Volume Workload.Volume.Mount _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod _.Area.Container" slug="Mounts" help.yaml.injected_token_volume="# Added to every pod by the API server unless automountServiceAccountToken: false (name suffix is random)
volumes:
 - name: kube-api-access-b2cgt
 projected:
 defaultMode: 420
 sources:
 - serviceAccountToken:
 expirationSeconds: 3607
 path: token
 - configMap:
 items:
 - key: ca.crt
 path: ca.crt
 name: kube-root-ca.crt
 - downwardAPI:
 items:
 - fieldRef:
 apiVersion: v1
 fieldPath: metadata.namespace
 path: namespace
volumeMounts:
 - mountPath: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount
 name: kube-api-access-b2cgt
 readOnly: true"/>
g.data-help:
Mounted volumes and env-vars
External data is often injected into pods via environment variables or projected volumes. These are typically read-only and can include ConfigMaps, Secrets, or dynamic runtime values like the pod IP or namespace.
When a pod needs to interact with the Kubernetes API, a service account token is automatically mounted as a projected volume. Ensure proper RBAC scoping for the associated service account to avoid privilege escalation.
g.data-help.yaml.injected_token_volume: # Added to every pod by the API server unless automountServiceAccountToken: false (name suffix is random) volumes: - name: kube-api-access-b2cgt projected: defaultMode: 420 sources: - serviceAccountToken: expirationSeconds: 3607 path: token - configMap: items: - key: ca.crt path: ca.crt name: kube-root-ca.crt - downwardAPI: items: - fieldRef: apiVersion: v1 fieldPath: metadata.namespace path: namespace volumeMounts: - mountPath: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount name: kube-api-access-b2cgt readOnly: true

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Internal pod egress

Egress traffic from a pod to other services inside the cluster can be controlled using NetworkPolicies, similar to ingress rules. However, egress rules are often overlooked, as ingress is more commonly enforced.

Define explicit egress policies to restrict which services a pod can communicate with, reducing lateral movement and attack surface in case of compromise." tags="level-1 pri-2 Network Network.Egress _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="PodEgress" help.yaml.allow_internal_calls="# storefront may only call catalog, cart, search and checkout on 8080, plus DNS; any other egress is dropped
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
 name: storefront-egress
 namespace: shop
spec:
 podSelector:
 matchLabels:
 app: storefront
 policyTypes:
 - Egress
 egress:
 - to:
 - podSelector:
 matchExpressions:
 - key: app
 operator: In
 values: ["catalog", "cart", "search", "checkout"]
 ports:
 - protocol: TCP
 port: 8080
 - to:
 - namespaceSelector:
 matchLabels:
 kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
 podSelector:
 matchLabels:
 k8s-app: kube-dns
 ports:
 - protocol: UDP
 port: 53
 - protocol: TCP
 port: 53"/>
g.data-help:
Internal pod egress
Egress traffic from a pod to other services inside the cluster can be controlled using NetworkPolicies, similar to ingress rules. However, egress rules are often overlooked, as ingress is more commonly enforced.
Define explicit egress policies to restrict which services a pod can communicate with, reducing lateral movement and attack surface in case of compromise.
g.data-help.yaml.allow_internal_calls: # storefront may only call catalog, cart, search and checkout on 8080, plus DNS; any other egress is dropped apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: name: storefront-egress namespace: shop spec: podSelector: matchLabels: app: storefront policyTypes: - Egress egress: - to: - podSelector: matchExpressions: - key: app operator: In values: ["catalog", "cart", "search", "checkout"] ports: - protocol: TCP port: 8080 - to: - namespaceSelector: matchLabels: kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system podSelector: matchLabels: k8s-app: kube-dns ports: - protocol: UDP port: 53 - protocol: TCP port: 53

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Secrets and ConfigMaps

Secrets and ConfigMaps can be encrypted at rest using encryption providers configured on the API server. The decryption keys are typically stored inside the cluster, often on disk.

For improved security, use external KMS providers (e.g., HashiCorp Vault, AWS KMS) to manage keys and prevent key compromise within the cluster." tags="level-2 pri-2 Workload Workload.Volume Workload.Volume.Source _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="CmSecret" help.yaml.kms_encryption_at_rest="# kube-apiserver --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
# Secrets are encrypted by a KMS v2 plugin; identity still reads older unencrypted data
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
 - resources:
 - secrets
 providers:
 - kms:
 apiVersion: v2
 name: vault-kms
 endpoint: unix:///var/run/kms-plugin/socket.sock
 timeout: 3s
 - identity: {}"/>
g.data-help:
Secrets and ConfigMaps
Secrets and ConfigMaps can be encrypted at rest using encryption providers configured on the API server. The decryption keys are typically stored inside the cluster, often on disk.
For improved security, use external KMS providers (e.g., HashiCorp Vault, AWS KMS) to manage keys and prevent key compromise within the cluster.
g.data-help.yaml.kms_encryption_at_rest: # kube-apiserver --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml # Secrets are encrypted by a KMS v2 plugin; identity still reads older unencrypted data apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1 kind: EncryptionConfiguration resources: - resources: - secrets providers: - kms: apiVersion: v2 name: vault-kms endpoint: unix:///var/run/kms-plugin/socket.sock timeout: 3s - identity: {}

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="system:masters group

The 'system:masters' group is a built-in Kubernetes group that bypasses the authorization layer and grants full administrative access to the cluster.

It should only be used for initial bootstrapping or controlled RBAC testing.
Ensure no regular users or service accounts are members of this group.
Monitor and audit usage carefully—this group should be empty in production environments." tags="level-3 pri-2 Api Api.Authn Api.Authz Api.Admission _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Api" slug="SystemMasters"/>
g.data-help:
system:masters group
The 'system:masters' group is a built-in Kubernetes group that bypasses the authorization layer and grants full administrative access to the cluster.
It should only be used for initial bootstrapping or controlled RBAC testing. Ensure no regular users or service accounts are members of this group. Monitor and audit usage carefully—this group should be empty in production environments.
g.data-tags: level-3 pri-2 Api Api.Authn Api.Authz Api.Admission _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Api

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Operators and Infrastructure Workloads

Operators act on custom Kubernetes resources (e.g., Certificates) via standard controllers. They typically run as Deployments and require RBAC access to specific APIs.

Treat operators like any other workload: apply strict access controls, run them on dedicated nodes if needed, and isolate privileges based on least privilege principles." tags="level-1 pri-2 CertManager CertManager.Issuer _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.CertManager" slug="CertManager" help.yaml.certificate_from_vault="# ClusterIssuer signs with Vault PKI; the Certificate keeps Secret shop-fjordmart-tls renewed
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
 name: vault-pki
spec:
 vault:
 server: https://vault.fjordmart.example
 path: pki_int/sign/fjordmart-example
 auth:
 kubernetes:
 role: cert-manager
 mountPath: /v1/auth/k8s-prod
 serviceAccountRef:
 name: cert-manager-vault
---
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
 name: shop-fjordmart-tls
 namespace: shop
spec:
 secretName: shop-fjordmart-tls
 dnsNames:
 - shop.fjordmart.example
 - www.fjordmart.example
 duration: 2160h
 renewBefore: 360h
 privateKey:
 algorithm: ECDSA
 size: 256
 rotationPolicy: Always
 issuerRef:
 group: cert-manager.io
 kind: ClusterIssuer
 name: vault-pki"/>
g.data-help:
Operators and Infrastructure Workloads
Operators act on custom Kubernetes resources (e.g., Certificates) via standard controllers. They typically run as Deployments and require RBAC access to specific APIs.
Treat operators like any other workload: apply strict access controls, run them on dedicated nodes if needed, and isolate privileges based on least privilege principles.
g.data-help.yaml.certificate_from_vault: # ClusterIssuer signs with Vault PKI; the Certificate keeps Secret shop-fjordmart-tls renewed apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1 kind: ClusterIssuer metadata: name: vault-pki spec: vault: server: https://vault.fjordmart.example path: pki_int/sign/fjordmart-example auth: kubernetes: role: cert-manager mountPath: /v1/auth/k8s-prod serviceAccountRef: name: cert-manager-vault --- apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1 kind: Certificate metadata: name: shop-fjordmart-tls namespace: shop spec: secretName: shop-fjordmart-tls dnsNames: - shop.fjordmart.example - www.fjordmart.example duration: 2160h renewBefore: 360h privateKey: algorithm: ECDSA size: 256 rotationPolicy: Always issuerRef: group: cert-manager.io kind: ClusterIssuer name: vault-pki

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Kubernetes Distributions and OS Choices

Choose a Kubernetes distribution and OS designed for security and minimal attack surface. Avoid general-purpose OSes that require separate patching.

Consider immutable, minimal, and hardened distros (e.g., Talos, Flatcar, Bottlerocket) purpose-built for Kubernetes production environments." tags="level-1 pri-2" slug="K8sDistro" help.shell.node_os_and_runtime="# OS image, kernel and container runtime per node
$ kubectl get nodes -o wide
NAME STATUS ROLES AGE VERSION INTERNAL-IP EXTERNAL-IP OS-IMAGE KERNEL-VERSION CONTAINER-RUNTIME
master-01 Ready control-plane 418d v1.34.1 10.20.1.11 <none> Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS 6.8.0-85-generic containerd://2.1.4
worker-03 Ready <none> 212d v1.34.1 10.20.4.17 <none> Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS 6.8.0-85-generic containerd://2.1.4
worker-05 Ready <none> 212d v1.34.1 10.20.4.19 <none> Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS 6.8.0-85-generic containerd://2.1.4"/>

Kubernetes Distributions and OS Choices
Choose a Kubernetes distribution and OS designed for security and minimal attack surface. Avoid general-purpose OSes that require separate patching.
Consider immutable, minimal, and hardened distros (e.g., Talos, Flatcar, Bottlerocket) purpose-built for Kubernetes production environments.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="GatewayAPI Policy Attachment

Policies add behavior to Gateway API resources, such as authentication, authorization, rate limiting, header manipulation, or security controls.

A policy usually attaches to a target resource (for example a Gateway or a Route) using a targetRef. The exact policy kinds and supported targets depend on the Gateway implementation.

Use policies to separate traffic routing (*Route) from operational and security concerns." tags="level-3 pri-2 Ingress Ingress.GatewayApi Ingress.GatewayApi.Policy _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="GatewayPolicy" help.yaml.rate_limit_route="# kgateway TrafficPolicy on HTTPRoute storefront: local rate limit, 100 requests/s, burst 200
apiVersion: gateway.kgateway.dev/v1alpha1
kind: TrafficPolicy
metadata:
 name: storefront-ratelimit
 namespace: shop
spec:
 targetRefs:
 - group: gateway.networking.k8s.io
 kind: HTTPRoute
 name: storefront
 rateLimit:
 local:
 tokenBucket:
 maxTokens: 200
 tokensPerFill: 100
 fillInterval: 1s"/>
g.data-help:
GatewayAPI Policy Attachment
Policies add behavior to Gateway API resources, such as authentication, authorization, rate limiting, header manipulation, or security controls.
A policy usually attaches to a target resource (for example a Gateway or a Route) using a targetRef. The exact policy kinds and supported targets depend on the Gateway implementation.
Use policies to separate traffic routing (*Route) from operational and security concerns.
g.data-help.yaml.rate_limit_route: # kgateway TrafficPolicy on HTTPRoute storefront: local rate limit, 100 requests/s, burst 200 apiVersion: gateway.kgateway.dev/v1alpha1 kind: TrafficPolicy metadata: name: storefront-ratelimit namespace: shop spec: targetRefs: - group: gateway.networking.k8s.io kind: HTTPRoute name: storefront rateLimit: local: tokenBucket: maxTokens: 200 tokensPerFill: 100 fillInterval: 1s

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Cross-Namespace Reference Permission (ReferenceGrant)

ReferenceGrant allows a resource in one namespace to reference a resource in another namespace, when the Gateway API would otherwise deny that cross-namespace reference.

It is typically used when a Route in one namespace points to a backend Service in another namespace.

The ReferenceGrant must be created in the target namespace (the namespace of the referenced resource), and it explicitly allows which resource kinds/namespaces may reference it." tags="level-3 pri-2 Ingress Ingress.GatewayApi Ingress.GatewayApi.Route _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="ReferenceGrant" help.yaml.allow_cross_namespace_secret="# Lives in shop: lets Gateways in gateway-system use Secret shop-fjordmart-tls
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: ReferenceGrant
metadata:
 name: gateway-system-tls
 namespace: shop
spec:
 from:
 - group: gateway.networking.k8s.io
 kind: Gateway
 namespace: gateway-system
 to:
 - group: ""
 kind: Secret
 name: shop-fjordmart-tls"/>
g.data-help:
Cross-Namespace Reference Permission (ReferenceGrant)
ReferenceGrant allows a resource in one namespace to reference a resource in another namespace, when the Gateway API would otherwise deny that cross-namespace reference.
It is typically used when a Route in one namespace points to a backend Service in another namespace.
The ReferenceGrant must be created in the target namespace (the namespace of the referenced resource), and it explicitly allows which resource kinds/namespaces may reference it.
g.data-help.yaml.allow_cross_namespace_sec: # Lives in shop: lets Gateways in gateway-system use Secret shop-fjordmart-tls apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: ReferenceGrant metadata: name: gateway-system-tls namespace: shop spec: from: - group: gateway.networking.k8s.io kind: Gateway namespace: gateway-system to: - group: "" kind: Secret name: shop-fjordmart-tls

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Custom Operators / orchestrators

Properly designed custom operators can enhance security by integrating tightly with Kubernetes-native patterns like RBAC, admission control, and CRDs.

For example, you can expose a custom resource that developers use to request infrastructure, while the operator enforces policy-compliant templates and behavior.
Operators can also manage resources external to the cluster in a controlled and auditable way." tags="level-2 pri-3 CustomOperator _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.CustomOperator" slug="CustomOperators"/>
g.data-help:
Custom Operators / orchestrators
Properly designed custom operators can enhance security by integrating tightly with Kubernetes-native patterns like RBAC, admission control, and CRDs.
For example, you can expose a custom resource that developers use to request infrastructure, while the operator enforces policy-compliant templates and behavior. Operators can also manage resources external to the cluster in a controlled and auditable way.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Exposed port

All containers in a pod share the same network namespace and run on the same node.
This allows enforcement of eBPF-based filters and transparent mTLS at the network level.

With sidecars or service mesh integration, unencrypted ports like 80 can safely be exposed internally. Encryption, authentication, and access control are handled outside the application, making this a secure and preferred approach for internal services." tags="level-2 pri-3 Network Network.Service Network.Service.Port _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod" slug="ExposedPorts" help.yaml.expose_port="# Service port 80 forwards to the container port named http
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
 name: storefront
 namespace: shop
spec:
 type: ClusterIP
 clusterIP: 10.96.12.40
 selector:
 app: storefront
 ports:
 - name: http
 port: 80
 targetPort: http"/>
g.data-help:
Exposed port
All containers in a pod share the same network namespace and run on the same node. This allows enforcement of eBPF-based filters and transparent mTLS at the network level.
With sidecars or service mesh integration, unencrypted ports like 80 can safely be exposed internally. Encryption, authentication, and access control are handled outside the application, making this a secure and preferred approach for internal services.
g.data-help.yaml.expose_port: # Service port 80 forwards to the container port named http apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: storefront namespace: shop spec: type: ClusterIP clusterIP: 10.96.12.40 selector: app: storefront ports: - name: http port: 80 targetPort: http

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Sidecar container

Sidecar containers can improve security by isolating responsibilities such as TLS termination, authentication, or logging from the main app. They are used by some service meshes (e.g., Istio), but newer approaches like eBPF and ambient meshes offer lower overhead and better scalability.

Sidecars share the same network namespace, allowing secure localhost (127.0.0.1) communication.
They can also enforce policies or proxy traffic, but increase attack surface and resource usage." tags="level-1 pri-3 Workload Workload.ContainerType Workload.ContainerType.Sidecar _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod" slug="Sidecar"/>
g.data-help:
Sidecar container
Sidecar containers can improve security by isolating responsibilities such as TLS termination, authentication, or logging from the main app. They are used by some service meshes (e.g., Istio), but newer approaches like eBPF and ambient meshes offer lower overhead and better scalability.
Sidecars share the same network namespace, allowing secure localhost (127.0.0.1) communication. They can also enforce policies or proxy traffic, but increase attack surface and resource usage.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Init container

Init containers enhance security by performing setup tasks before the main container starts, such as validating configs, downloading secrets, or verifying service dependencies.

They run with separate images and permissions, reducing attack surface in the main container.
Types include wait-for-dependency containers, secret fetchers, permission fixers (e.g., chown volumes), and environment validators. Since they run sequentially and exit before app start, they can enforce strict preconditions and avoid persistent exposure." tags="level-1 pri-3 Workload Workload.ContainerType Workload.ContainerType.Init _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod" slug="InitContainer" help.yaml.wait_for_database="# Init container waits until checkout-db answers on 5432, with fewer privileges than the app
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
 name: checkout
 namespace: shop
spec:
 initContainers:
 - name: wait-for-db
 image: registry.fjordmart.example/base/busybox:1.37
 command: ["sh", "-c", "until nc -z -w 2 checkout-db 5432; do sleep 2; done"]
 securityContext:
 runAsNonRoot: true
 runAsUser: 65532
 allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
 readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
 capabilities:
 drop: ["ALL"]
 containers:
 - name: checkout
 image: registry.fjordmart.example/shop/checkout:3.2.4"/>
g.data-help:
Init container
Init containers enhance security by performing setup tasks before the main container starts, such as validating configs, downloading secrets, or verifying service dependencies.
They run with separate images and permissions, reducing attack surface in the main container. Types include wait-for-dependency containers, secret fetchers, permission fixers (e.g., chown volumes), and environment validators. Since they run sequentially and exit before app start, they can enforce strict preconditions and avoid persistent exposure.
g.data-help.yaml.wait_for_database: # Init container waits until checkout-db answers on 5432, with fewer privileges than the app apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: checkout namespace: shop spec: initContainers: - name: wait-for-db image: registry.fjordmart.example/base/busybox:1.37 command: ["sh", "-c", "until nc -z -w 2 checkout-db 5432; do sleep 2; done"] securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true runAsUser: 65532 allowPrivilegeEscalation: false readOnlyRootFilesystem: true capabilities: drop: ["ALL"] containers: - name: checkout image: registry.fjordmart.example/shop/checkout:3.2.4

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Ephemeral containers

Ephemeral containers are used for live debugging of running Pods without restarting them.
They provide no guarantees on lifecycle, don't support volumes, and can't be part of normal app logic.
From a security standpoint, they are powerful but risky—if enabled, they allow runtime inspection, so access should be tightly controlled (e.g., via RBAC).

They share namespaces (like network and PID) with existing containers, enabling deep introspection but also potential abuse if misused." tags="level-2 pri-3 Workload Workload.ContainerType Workload.ContainerType.Ephemeral _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod" slug="Ephemeral" help.shell.debug_running_pod="# Adds a debug container to a running pod; --target shares the process namespace of container storefront
$ kubectl debug -n shop -it storefront-6c9fd4d8b7-x2n4k --image=registry.fjordmart.example/platform/debug:1.4.0 --target=storefront --profile=restricted -- sh"/>
g.data-help:
Ephemeral containers
Ephemeral containers are used for live debugging of running Pods without restarting them. They provide no guarantees on lifecycle, don't support volumes, and can't be part of normal app logic. From a security standpoint, they are powerful but risky—if enabled, they allow runtime inspection, so access should be tightly controlled (e.g., via RBAC).
They share namespaces (like network and PID) with existing containers, enabling deep introspection but also potential abuse if misused.
g.data-help.shell.debug_running_pod: # Adds a debug container to a running pod; --target shares the process namespace of container storefront $ kubectl debug -n shop -it storefront-6c9fd4d8b7-x2n4k --image=registry.fjordmart.example/platform/debug:1.4.0 --target=storefront --profile=restricted -- sh

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="WASM containers

WASM containers aim to run WebAssembly modules in place of traditional OCI containers, offering stronger isolation, faster cold starts, and lower resource usage. They don't rely on Linux syscalls, reducing attack surface and making them ideal for sandboxed, untrusted code. Projects like wasmEdge, containerd-shim-wasmedge, and Krustlet explore this in Kubernetes.

Long-term, WASM containers could enable safer multi-tenant workloads and portable compute across cloud, edge, and browser environments." tags="level-2 pri-3 Workload Workload.ContainerType Workload.ContainerType.Wasm _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod" slug="Wasm"/>
g.data-help:
WASM containers
WASM containers aim to run WebAssembly modules in place of traditional OCI containers, offering stronger isolation, faster cold starts, and lower resource usage. They don't rely on Linux syscalls, reducing attack surface and making them ideal for sandboxed, untrusted code. Projects like wasmEdge, containerd-shim-wasmedge, and Krustlet explore this in Kubernetes.
Long-term, WASM containers could enable safer multi-tenant workloads and portable compute across cloud, edge, and browser environments.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Hardened container runtimes

Hardened container runtimes provide additional isolation layers beyond standard runtimes like runc. For example, gVisor intercepts syscalls and provides a userspace kernel implementation, while Kata Containers wrap each container in lightweight virtual machines.

OpenShift Sandbox Containers use Kata under the hood to offer enhanced isolation." tags="level-3 pri-3 Workload Workload.Sandbox _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod" slug="HardenedRuntime" help.yaml.run_pod_in_gvisor="# Pods with runtimeClassName gvisor run in gVisor (runsc) and are only scheduled to nodes that have it
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
 name: gvisor
handler: runsc
scheduling:
 nodeSelector:
 runtime.fjordmart.example/gvisor: "true"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
 name: search
 namespace: shop
spec:
 runtimeClassName: gvisor
 containers:
 - name: search
 image: registry.fjordmart.example/shop/search:2.0.1"/>
g.data-help:
Hardened container runtimes
Hardened container runtimes provide additional isolation layers beyond standard runtimes like runc. For example, gVisor intercepts syscalls and provides a userspace kernel implementation, while Kata Containers wrap each container in lightweight virtual machines.
OpenShift Sandbox Containers use Kata under the hood to offer enhanced isolation.
g.data-help.yaml.run_pod_in_gvisor: # Pods with runtimeClassName gvisor run in gVisor (runsc) and are only scheduled to nodes that have it apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1 kind: RuntimeClass metadata: name: gvisor handler: runsc scheduling: nodeSelector: runtime.fjordmart.example/gvisor: "true" --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: search namespace: shop spec: runtimeClassName: gvisor containers: - name: search image: registry.fjordmart.example/shop/search:2.0.1

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="VirtualMachine or other workload-types

Other workload types, such as VirtualMachines (e.g., via KubeVirt), follow the same security mechanisms as pods: RBAC, network policies, storage classes, and admission control.

They are not inherently more privileged and should be treated like any other workload with proper isolation, policy enforcement, and monitoring in place." tags="level-1 pri-3 Workload Workload.Vm _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment" slug="Vm"/>
g.data-help:
VirtualMachine or other workload-types
Other workload types, such as VirtualMachines (e.g., via KubeVirt), follow the same security mechanisms as pods: RBAC, network policies, storage classes, and admission control.
They are not inherently more privileged and should be treated like any other workload with proper isolation, policy enforcement, and monitoring in place.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Authentication webhook

Authentication webhooks are less commonly used, but can provide additional control beyond standard RBAC. They allow dynamic authentication decisions based on external systems or custom logic.

For example, a webhook can reject requests targeting namespaces that match certain patterns or enforce organization-specific access rules in real time." tags="level-3 pri-3 Api Api.Authn Api.Authn.Webhook _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="AuthWebhook"/>
g.data-help:
Authentication webhook
Authentication webhooks are less commonly used, but can provide additional control beyond standard RBAC. They allow dynamic authentication decisions based on external systems or custom logic.
For example, a webhook can reject requests targeting namespaces that match certain patterns or enforce organization-specific access rules in real time.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Cluster to cluster mesh (cluster-mesh)

A cluster-mesh connects multiple Kubernetes clusters to enable cross-cluster communication with cloud-native networking features. This allows services in different clusters to communicate as if they were in the same network.

Traffic can be encrypted using mTLS and authenticated using workload identities unique to each cluster. With proper setup, standard Kubernetes NetworkPolicies can be enforced across cluster boundaries." tags="level-2 pri-3 Network Network.ClusterMesh" slug="ClusterMesh"/>
g.data-help:
Cluster to cluster mesh (cluster-mesh)
A cluster-mesh connects multiple Kubernetes clusters to enable cross-cluster communication with cloud-native networking features. This allows services in different clusters to communicate as if they were in the same network.
Traffic can be encrypted using mTLS and authenticated using workload identities unique to each cluster. With proper setup, standard Kubernetes NetworkPolicies can be enforced across cluster boundaries.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="etcd

etcd stores the entire state of the Kubernetes cluster and must be protected accordingly.
Enable encryption at rest using the API server's encryption provider configuration.

Access to etcd should be strictly limited to the API server. Ensure mutual TLS is enabled, and never expose etcd directly to the network." tags="level-3 pri-3 ControlPlane ControlPlane.Etcd _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="Etcd"/>
g.data-help:
etcd
etcd stores the entire state of the Kubernetes cluster and must be protected accordingly. Enable encryption at rest using the API server's encryption provider configuration.
Access to etcd should be strictly limited to the API server. Ensure mutual TLS is enabled, and never expose etcd directly to the network.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Validating and Mutating Admission Control

Admission controllers intercept API requests after authentication and authorization, allowing for policy enforcement. Tools like Kyverno and OPA Gatekeeper can validate incoming YAML against cluster policies or mutate it to enforce configuration standards (e.g., securityContext, labels, resource limits).

All resources—user-submitted or system-generated—must pass admission control.
These controllers can also enforce image signature verification (e.g., cosign) and SLSA provenance checks to prevent untrusted artifacts from being deployed." tags="level-2 pri-2 Api Api.Admission _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Api" slug="AdmissionControl" help.yaml.allow_only_internal_images="# Rejects pods and debug containers in shop whose image is not from registry.fjordmart.example
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
 name: internal-registry-only
spec:
 failurePolicy: Fail
 matchConstraints:
 resourceRules:
 - apiGroups: [""]
 apiVersions: ["v1"]
 operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
 resources: ["pods", "pods/ephemeralcontainers"]
 variables:
 - name: containers
 expression: >-
 object.spec.containers +
 object.spec.?initContainers.orValue([]) +
 object.spec.?ephemeralContainers.orValue([])
 validations:
 - expression: >-
 variables.containers.all(c, c.image.startsWith('registry.fjordmart.example/'))
 messageExpression: >-
 'image not from registry.fjordmart.example: ' +
 variables.containers.filter(c, !c.image.startsWith('registry.fjordmart.example/')).map(c, c.image).join(', ')
 reason: Forbidden
---
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding
metadata:
 name: internal-registry-only-shop
spec:
 policyName: internal-registry-only
 validationActions: ["Deny", "Audit"]
 matchResources:
 namespaceSelector:
 matchLabels:
 kubernetes.io/metadata.name: shop" help.log.rejected_pod="# Pod with image docker.io/library/debian created in namespace shop
$ kubectl --token="$STOLEN_TOKEN" create -f cache-warmer.yaml
Error from server (Forbidden): error when creating "cache-warmer.yaml": pods "cache-warmer" is forbidden: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy 'internal-registry-only' with binding 'internal-registry-only-shop' denied request: image not from registry.fjordmart.example: docker.io/library/debian"/>
g.data-help:
Validating and Mutating Admission Control
Admission controllers intercept API requests after authentication and authorization, allowing for policy enforcement. Tools like Kyverno and OPA Gatekeeper can validate incoming YAML against cluster policies or mutate it to enforce configuration standards (e.g., securityContext, labels, resource limits).
All resources—user-submitted or system-generated—must pass admission control. These controllers can also enforce image signature verification (e.g., cosign) and SLSA provenance checks to prevent untrusted artifacts from being deployed.
g.data-help.yaml.allow_only_internal_image: # Rejects pods and debug containers in shop whose image is not from registry.fjordmart.example apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1 kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy metadata: name: internal-registry-only spec: failurePolicy: Fail matchConstraints: resourceRules: - apiGroups: [""] apiVersions: ["v1"] operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"] resources: ["pods", "pods/ephemeralcontainers"] variables: - name: containers expression: >- object.spec.containers + object.spec.?initContainers.orValue([]) + object.spec.?ephemeralContainers.orValue([]) validations: - expression: >- variables.containers.all(c, c.image.startsWith('registry.fjordmart.example/')) messageExpression: >- 'image not from registry.fjordmart.example: ' + variables.containers.filter(c, !c.image.startsWith('registry.fjordmart.example/')).map(c, c.image).join(', ') reason: Forbidden --- apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1 kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding metadata: name: internal-registry-only-shop spec: policyName: internal-registry-only validationActions: ["Deny", "Audit"] matchResources: namespaceSelector: matchLabels: kubernetes.io/metadata.name: shop
g.data-help.log.rejected_pod: # Pod with image docker.io/library/debian created in namespace shop $ kubectl --token="$STOLEN_TOKEN" create -f cache-warmer.yaml Error from server (Forbidden): error when creating "cache-warmer.yaml": pods "cache-warmer" is forbidden: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy 'internal-registry-only' with binding 'internal-registry-only-shop' denied request: image not from registry.fjordmart.example: docker.io/library/debian

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="font-size: 18px; color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b style="">?</b></font>" help="System call filtering (Seccomp)

A pod can restrict which Linux system calls are available to containers using seccomp.
This reduces the kernel attack surface by blocking system calls that are not required by the workload.

Kubernetes does not apply system call filtering by default unless seccomp defaulting is enabled on the nodes.
A pod can explicitly use the runtime’s default seccomp profile or a custom profile for more restrictive filtering." tags="level-3 info ProcessSecurity ProcessSecurity.Seccomp _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod _.Area.Container _.Area.Process _.Area.KernelSecurity" slug="Seccomp" help.shell.check_seccomp_mode="# Seccomp 0 = no filter, 2 = filter active
$ kubectl exec -n shop cache-warmer -- grep Seccomp /proc/1/status
Seccomp:	0
Seccomp_filters:	0
# storefront (seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault)
Seccomp:	2
Seccomp_filters:	1"/>
g.data-help:
System call filtering (Seccomp)
A pod can restrict which Linux system calls are available to containers using seccomp. This reduces the kernel attack surface by blocking system calls that are not required by the workload.
Kubernetes does not apply system call filtering by default unless seccomp defaulting is enabled on the nodes. A pod can explicitly use the runtime’s default seccomp profile or a custom profile for more restrictive filtering.
g.data-help.shell.check_seccomp_mode: # Seccomp 0 = no filter, 2 = filter active $ kubectl exec -n shop cache-warmer -- grep Seccomp /proc/1/status Seccomp: 0 Seccomp_filters: 0 # storefront (seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault) Seccomp: 2 Seccomp_filters: 1

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Network interfaces (overlay)

Normal kubernetes network is done using an overlay using a CNI (Container Network Interface), like Cilium, Flannel, Calico and many others. They have various functionality and security.
Example, some CNIs doesnt support egress network policies, some uses eBPF a lot, some iptables." tags="level-3 pri-2 Network Network.Cni _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod" slug="Overlay"/>
g.data-help:
Network interfaces (overlay)
Normal kubernetes network is done using an overlay using a CNI (Container Network Interface), like Cilium, Flannel, Calico and many others. They have various functionality and security. Example, some CNIs doesnt support egress network policies, some uses eBPF a lot, some iptables.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="API Priority and Fairness (APF)

API Priority and Fairness controls how incoming API requests are prioritized and rate-limited.
Requests are classified into priority levels based on attributes such as the authenticated user, group, or request type.

This protects the API server from overload while ensuring that important requests receive sufficient resources during periods of high demand." tags="level-2 pri-3 Api Api.Apf _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Api" slug="Apf" help.yaml.rate_limit_serviceaccounts="# All ServiceAccounts in shop share one limited, queued priority level
apiVersion: flowcontrol.apiserver.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityLevelConfiguration
metadata:
 name: shop-workloads
spec:
 type: Limited
 limited:
 nominalConcurrencyShares: 10
 lendablePercent: 0
 limitResponse:
 type: Queue
 queuing:
 queues: 16
 handSize: 4
 queueLengthLimit: 50
---
apiVersion: flowcontrol.apiserver.k8s.io/v1
kind: FlowSchema
metadata:
 name: shop-serviceaccounts
spec:
 priorityLevelConfiguration:
 name: shop-workloads
 matchingPrecedence: 1000
 distinguisherMethod:
 type: ByUser
 rules:
 - subjects:
 - kind: Group
 group:
 name: system:serviceaccounts:shop
 resourceRules:
 - verbs: ["*"]
 apiGroups: ["*"]
 resources: ["*"]
 namespaces: ["*"]
 clusterScope: true
 nonResourceRules:
 - verbs: ["*"]
 nonResourceURLs: ["*"]"/>
g.data-help:
API Priority and Fairness (APF)
API Priority and Fairness controls how incoming API requests are prioritized and rate-limited. Requests are classified into priority levels based on attributes such as the authenticated user, group, or request type.
This protects the API server from overload while ensuring that important requests receive sufficient resources during periods of high demand.
g.data-help.yaml.rate_limit_serviceaccount: # All ServiceAccounts in shop share one limited, queued priority level apiVersion: flowcontrol.apiserver.k8s.io/v1 kind: PriorityLevelConfiguration metadata: name: shop-workloads spec: type: Limited limited: nominalConcurrencyShares: 10 lendablePercent: 0 limitResponse: type: Queue queuing: queues: 16 handSize: 4 queueLengthLimit: 50 --- apiVersion: flowcontrol.apiserver.k8s.io/v1 kind: FlowSchema metadata: name: shop-serviceaccounts spec: priorityLevelConfiguration: name: shop-workloads matchingPrecedence: 1000 distinguisherMethod: type: ByUser rules: - subjects: - kind: Group group: name: system:serviceaccounts:shop resourceRules: - verbs: ["*"] apiGroups: ["*"] resources: ["*"] namespaces: ["*"] clusterScope: true nonResourceRules: - verbs: ["*"] nonResourceURLs: ["*"]

g.content: <UserObject label="" tags="level-3 Api Api.Authz Api.Rbac Api.Rbac.Binding _ _.Line _.Line.BelongsTo _.Item _.Item.Rbac _.Item.ClusterRoleBinding _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Api _.Area.Rbac _.Link _.Link.RbacToClusterRoleBinding"/>

<UserObject label="" help="API to etcd Communication

The Kubernetes API server communicates with etcd to persist cluster state.
Read operations (e.g., GET) fetch data directly and do not trigger admission controllers.

Kubernetes also includes the built-in Pod Security Admission (PSA) controller, which enforces the Pod Security Standards (privileged, baseline, restricted) on all created or updated Pods without requiring external webhooks/controllers (it's builtin to the apiserver).

Admission controllers only intercept mutating operations (e.g., CREATE, UPDATE, DELETE).
This means read access must be tightly controlled via RBAC/ABAC, since policies cannot be enforced via admission webhooks for those requests." tags="level-3 pri-2 Api ControlPlane ControlPlane.Etcd _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="ApiToEtcd"/>
g.data-help:
API to etcd Communication
The Kubernetes API server communicates with etcd to persist cluster state. Read operations (e.g., GET) fetch data directly and do not trigger admission controllers.
Kubernetes also includes the built-in Pod Security Admission (PSA) controller, which enforces the Pod Security Standards (privileged, baseline, restricted) on all created or updated Pods without requiring external webhooks/controllers (it's builtin to the apiserver).
Admission controllers only intercept mutating operations (e.g., CREATE, UPDATE, DELETE). This means read access must be tightly controlled via RBAC/ABAC, since policies cannot be enforced via admission webhooks for those requests.

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="font-size: 18px; color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b style="">?</b></font>" help="Mandatory Access Control (MAC)

Mandatory Access Control restricts which resources and operations are available to processes based on security policies enforced by the Linux kernel.
This provides an additional security layer beyond traditional Unix permissions and capabilities, limiting what a compromised container can access even when normal permissions would allow it.

In Kubernetes, MAC can be enforced using Linux Security Modules such as AppArmor or SELinux.
The available mechanism and its enforcement depend on the operating system and security configuration of the Kubernetes nodes." tags="level-3 info ProcessSecurity ProcessSecurity.Mac _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod _.Area.Container _.Area.Process _.Area.KernelSecurity" slug="Mac"/>
g.data-help:
Mandatory Access Control (MAC)
Mandatory Access Control restricts which resources and operations are available to processes based on security policies enforced by the Linux kernel. This provides an additional security layer beyond traditional Unix permissions and capabilities, limiting what a compromised container can access even when normal permissions would allow it.
In Kubernetes, MAC can be enforced using Linux Security Modules such as AppArmor or SELinux. The available mechanism and its enforcement depend on the operating system and security configuration of the Kubernetes nodes.

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="font-size: 18px; color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b style="">?</b></font>" help="AppArmor

A pod can restrict which resources and operations are available to containers using AppArmor.
This limits what a compromised process can access, such as files, capabilities, networking, and other kernel-controlled resources.

AppArmor enforcement depends on AppArmor being enabled and supported on the nodes.
A pod can explicitly use the runtime’s default AppArmor profile or a custom profile for more restrictive access control." tags="level-3 info ProcessSecurity ProcessSecurity.Mac _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod _.Area.Container _.Area.Process _.Area.KernelSecurity" slug="AppArmor" help.shell.check_active_profile="# AppArmor profile of the container's main process; attr/apparmor/ is AppArmor-only, so SELinux can't show up here
$ kubectl exec -n shop cache-warmer -- cat /proc/1/attr/apparmor/current
cri-containerd.apparmor.d (enforce)" help.yaml.enable_default_profile="# Run the pod's containers under the container runtime's default AppArmor profile
spec:
 securityContext:
 appArmorProfile:
 type: RuntimeDefault"/>
g.data-help:
AppArmor
A pod can restrict which resources and operations are available to containers using AppArmor. This limits what a compromised process can access, such as files, capabilities, networking, and other kernel-controlled resources.
AppArmor enforcement depends on AppArmor being enabled and supported on the nodes. A pod can explicitly use the runtime’s default AppArmor profile or a custom profile for more restrictive access control.
g.data-help.shell.check_active_profile: # AppArmor profile of the container's main process; attr/apparmor/ is AppArmor-only, so SELinux can't show up here $ kubectl exec -n shop cache-warmer -- cat /proc/1/attr/apparmor/current cri-containerd.apparmor.d (enforce)
g.data-help.yaml.enable_default_profile: # Run the pod's containers under the container runtime's default AppArmor profile spec: securityContext: appArmorProfile: type: RuntimeDefault

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="font-size: 18px; color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b style="">?</b></font>" help="SELinux

A pod can restrict which resources and operations are available to containers using SELinux.
SELinux uses security labels and policies to control how container processes can interact with files, devices, processes, and other system resources.

SELinux enforcement depends on SELinux being enabled and configured on the nodes.
A pod can specify SELinux labels through its security context, while the actual access rules are defined by the SELinux policy installed on the node." tags="level-3 info ProcessSecurity ProcessSecurity.Mac _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod _.Area.Container _.Area.Process _.Area.KernelSecurity" slug="SeLinux" help.shell.container_process_labels="# On an SELinux node: container processes run as container_t, each pod with its own category pair
$ ps -eZ | grep container_t
system_u:system_r:container_t:s0:c295,c947 48731 ? 00:00:03 kworkerd
system_u:system_r:container_t:s0:c123,c456 51208 ? 00:01:12 search" help.yaml.fixed_mcs_level="# Fixed SELinux MCS level, e.g. so two pods sharing a volume get the same label (normally the runtime picks a random pair)
spec:
 securityContext:
 seLinuxOptions:
 level: "s0:c123,c456""/>

SELinux
A pod can restrict which resources and operations are available to containers using SELinux. SELinux uses security labels and policies to control how container processes can interact with files, devices, processes, and other system resources.
SELinux enforcement depends on SELinux being enabled and configured on the nodes. A pod can specify SELinux labels through its security context, while the actual access rules are defined by the SELinux policy installed on the node.

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="font-size: 18px; color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b style="">?</b></font>" help="Container Runtime Security Policies

A pod can restrict the privileges and runtime environment available to its containers using the Kubernetes security context.
These controls can limit container privileges, enforce user and group identities, restrict filesystem access, and reduce access to sensitive kernel functionality.

Runtime security policies can enforce non-root execution, specific user and group IDs, a read-only root filesystem, restricted Linux capabilities, limited /proc access, and prevention of privilege escalation or privileged execution.

These restrictions are configured at the pod or container level and are enforced by Kubernetes, the container runtime, and the underlying Linux kernel." tags="level-2 info ProcessSecurity ProcessSecurity.RunPolicy _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod _.Area.Container _.Area.Process" slug="RunPolicies" help.yaml.hardened_deployment="# Non-root, no capabilities, read-only root fs, RuntimeDefault seccomp/AppArmor, own user namespace
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
 name: storefront
 namespace: shop
spec:
 replicas: 4
 selector:
 matchLabels:
 app: storefront
 template:
 metadata:
 labels:
 app: storefront
 spec:
 serviceAccountName: storefront
 hostUsers: false
 securityContext:
 runAsNonRoot: true
 runAsUser: 65532
 runAsGroup: 65532
 seccompProfile:
 type: RuntimeDefault
 appArmorProfile:
 type: RuntimeDefault
 containers:
 - name: storefront
 image: registry.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront:2.8.1
 ports:
 - name: http
 containerPort: 8080
 securityContext:
 allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
 readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
 capabilities:
 drop: ["ALL"]
 volumeMounts:
 - name: tmp
 mountPath: /tmp
 volumes:
 - name: tmp
 emptyDir:
 medium: Memory
 sizeLimit: 64Mi"/>
g.data-help:
Container Runtime Security Policies
A pod can restrict the privileges and runtime environment available to its containers using the Kubernetes security context. These controls can limit container privileges, enforce user and group identities, restrict filesystem access, and reduce access to sensitive kernel functionality.
Runtime security policies can enforce non-root execution, specific user and group IDs, a read-only root filesystem, restricted Linux capabilities, limited /proc access, and prevention of privilege escalation or privileged execution.
These restrictions are configured at the pod or container level and are enforced by Kubernetes, the container runtime, and the underlying Linux kernel.
g.data-help.yaml.hardened_deployment: # Non-root, no capabilities, read-only root fs, RuntimeDefault seccomp/AppArmor, own user namespace apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: storefront namespace: shop spec: replicas: 4 selector: matchLabels: app: storefront template: metadata: labels: app: storefront spec: serviceAccountName: storefront hostUsers: false securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true runAsUser: 65532 runAsGroup: 65532 seccompProfile: type: RuntimeDefault appArmorProfile: type: RuntimeDefault containers: - name: storefront image: registry.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront:2.8.1 ports: - name: http containerPort: 8080 securityContext: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false readOnlyRootFilesystem: true capabilities: drop: ["ALL"] volumeMounts: - name: tmp mountPath: /tmp volumes: - name: tmp emptyDir: medium: Memory sizeLimit: 64Mi

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="font-size: 18px; color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b style="">?</b></font>" help="Pod-to-Pod Communication

Each pod has its own cluster IP address and can communicate directly with another pod using that IP.

Because pod IPs are ephemeral, applications normally connect through a Kubernetes Service using its DNS name. DNS resolves the name to the Service’s virtual ClusterIP, which is then translated or routed to one of the backend pod IPs.

Depending on the cluster networking implementation, Service forwarding and load balancing can be handled by kube-proxy using iptables/IPVS, or directly using eBPF.

Pod > Pod IP > Pod

Pod > Service DNS > ClusterIP > Backend Pod" tags="level-1 info Network Network.Egress Network.Service Network.PodToPod _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="InternalTraffic" help.shell.service_to_pod_ips="# Service ClusterIP and the pod IPs (EndpointSlice) behind it
$ kubectl get svc storefront -n shop
NAME TYPE CLUSTER-IP EXTERNAL-IP PORT(S) AGE
storefront ClusterIP 10.96.12.40 <none> 80/TCP 418d
$ kubectl get endpointslices -n shop -l kubernetes.io/service-name=storefront
NAME ADDRESSTYPE PORTS ENDPOINTS AGE
storefront-wdc8c IPv4 8080 10.244.1.23,10.244.2.31,10.244.4.17 + 1 more... 418d"/>
g.data-help:
Pod-to-Pod Communication
Each pod has its own cluster IP address and can communicate directly with another pod using that IP.
Because pod IPs are ephemeral, applications normally connect through a Kubernetes Service using its DNS name. DNS resolves the name to the Service’s virtual ClusterIP, which is then translated or routed to one of the backend pod IPs.
Depending on the cluster networking implementation, Service forwarding and load balancing can be handled by kube-proxy using iptables/IPVS, or directly using eBPF.
Pod > Pod IP > Pod
Pod > Service DNS > ClusterIP > Backend Pod
g.data-tags: level-1 info Network Network.Egress Network.Service Network.PodToPod _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster
g.data-help.shell.service_to_pod_ips: # Service ClusterIP and the pod IPs (EndpointSlice) behind it $ kubectl get svc storefront -n shop NAME TYPE CLUSTER-IP EXTERNAL-IP PORT(S) AGE storefront ClusterIP 10.96.12.40 <none> 80/TCP 418d $ kubectl get endpointslices -n shop -l kubernetes.io/service-name=storefront NAME ADDRESSTYPE PORTS ENDPOINTS AGE storefront-wdc8c IPv4 8080 10.244.1.23,10.244.2.31,10.244.4.17 + 1 more... 418d

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Linux Capabilities

Linux capabilities split traditional root privileges into smaller individual permissions that can be granted or removed from containers through the Kubernetes security context.

Common capabilities that can be restricted include NET_ADMIN for network configuration, NET_RAW for raw sockets, SYS_ADMIN for a broad range of administrative operations, SYS_PTRACE for process tracing, SYS_MODULE for kernel module operations, SYS_CHROOT for changing the root directory, MKNOD for creating device nodes, and CHOWN for changing file ownership.

Containers can drop individual capabilities or use drop: ["ALL"] and explicitly add back only the capabilities required by the workload." tags="level-3 pri-2 ProcessSecurity ProcessSecurity.RunPolicy ProcessSecurity.RunPolicy.Privilege _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod _.Area.Container _.Area.Process _.Area.RunPolicies" slug="Capabilities" help.shell.check_capabilities="# Effective capabilities: containerd default set vs. drop: ["ALL"]
$ kubectl exec -n shop cache-warmer -- grep CapEff /proc/1/status
CapEff:	00000000a80425fb
$ capsh --decode=00000000a80425fb
0x00000000a80425fb=cap_chown,cap_dac_override,cap_fowner,cap_fsetid,cap_kill,cap_setgid,cap_setuid,cap_setpcap,cap_net_bind_service,cap_net_raw,cap_sys_chroot,cap_mknod,cap_audit_write,cap_setfcap
# storefront (drop: ["ALL"])
CapEff:	0000000000000000"/>
g.data-help:
Linux Capabilities
Linux capabilities split traditional root privileges into smaller individual permissions that can be granted or removed from containers through the Kubernetes security context.
Common capabilities that can be restricted include NET_ADMIN for network configuration, NET_RAW for raw sockets, SYS_ADMIN for a broad range of administrative operations, SYS_PTRACE for process tracing, SYS_MODULE for kernel module operations, SYS_CHROOT for changing the root directory, MKNOD for creating device nodes, and CHOWN for changing file ownership.
Containers can drop individual capabilities or use drop: ["ALL"] and explicitly add back only the capabilities required by the workload.
g.data-help.shell.check_capabilities: # Effective capabilities: containerd default set vs. drop: ["ALL"] $ kubectl exec -n shop cache-warmer -- grep CapEff /proc/1/status CapEff: 00000000a80425fb $ capsh --decode=00000000a80425fb 0x00000000a80425fb=cap_chown,cap_dac_override,cap_fowner,cap_fsetid,cap_kill,cap_setgid,cap_setuid,cap_setpcap,cap_net_bind_service,cap_net_raw,cap_sys_chroot,cap_mknod,cap_audit_write,cap_setfcap # storefront (drop: ["ALL"]) CapEff: 0000000000000000

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Read-Only Root Filesystem

A container can be configured with a read-only root filesystem using the Kubernetes security context.

This prevents processes from modifying the container image filesystem, including application binaries, libraries, and configuration files.

Applications that require writable storage can use explicitly mounted volumes for directories such as temporary files, caches, logs, or persistent application data." tags="level-3 pri-2 ProcessSecurity ProcessSecurity.RunPolicy ProcessSecurity.RunPolicy.Filesystem _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod _.Area.Container _.Area.Process _.Area.RunPolicies" slug="ReadOnlyFs" help.yaml.read_only_root_with_tmp="# Root filesystem is read-only; /tmp is a small writable in-memory volume
securityContext:
 readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
volumeMounts:
 - name: tmp
 mountPath: /tmp
# ...
volumes:
 - name: tmp
 emptyDir:
 medium: Memory
 sizeLimit: 64Mi"/>
g.data-help:
Read-Only Root Filesystem
A container can be configured with a read-only root filesystem using the Kubernetes security context.
This prevents processes from modifying the container image filesystem, including application binaries, libraries, and configuration files.
Applications that require writable storage can use explicitly mounted volumes for directories such as temporary files, caches, logs, or persistent application data.
g.data-help.yaml.read_only_root_with_tmp: # Root filesystem is read-only; /tmp is a small writable in-memory volume securityContext: readOnlyRootFilesystem: true volumeMounts: - name: tmp mountPath: /tmp # ... volumes: - name: tmp emptyDir: medium: Memory sizeLimit: 64Mi

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Non-Root Execution

A container can be required to run as a non-root user using the Kubernetes security context.

The runAsNonRoot setting prevents the container from starting if its process would run as UID 0. A specific non-root user and group can also be enforced using runAsUser and runAsGroup.

This prevents workloads from running with root identity inside the container and reduces the privileges available to the application process." tags="level-3 pri-1 ProcessSecurity ProcessSecurity.RunPolicy ProcessSecurity.RunPolicy.User _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod _.Area.Container _.Area.Process _.Area.RunPolicies" slug="NoRoot" help.log.root_image_rejected="# Pod with runAsNonRoot: true, image docker.io/library/debian (runs as root)
$ kubectl get pod -n shop cache-warmer -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].state.waiting.message}'
container has runAsNonRoot and image will run as root (pod: "cache-warmer_shop(c4d4962a-173a-484b-a2cd-64bf8f054fa8)", container: cache-warmer)" help.yaml.require_non_root="# The container must not run as UID 0; runAsUser also lets the kubelet check images whose USER is a name
spec:
 securityContext:
 runAsNonRoot: true
 runAsUser: 65532
 runAsGroup: 65532"/>
g.data-help:
Non-Root Execution
A container can be required to run as a non-root user using the Kubernetes security context.
The runAsNonRoot setting prevents the container from starting if its process would run as UID 0. A specific non-root user and group can also be enforced using runAsUser and runAsGroup.
This prevents workloads from running with root identity inside the container and reduces the privileges available to the application process.
g.data-help.log.root_image_rejected: # Pod with runAsNonRoot: true, image docker.io/library/debian (runs as root) $ kubectl get pod -n shop cache-warmer -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].state.waiting.message}' container has runAsNonRoot and image will run as root (pod: "cache-warmer_shop(c4d4962a-173a-484b-a2cd-64bf8f054fa8)", container: cache-warmer)
g.data-help.yaml.require_non_root: # The container must not run as UID 0; runAsUser also lets the kubelet check images whose USER is a name spec: securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true runAsUser: 65532 runAsGroup: 65532

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Volume definitions

Pods can use different volume types, some of which may expose sensitive host resources to containers.

Volume types such as hostPath can provide direct access to the node filesystem and are commonly restricted in security-sensitive environments. Workloads should only be allowed to use volume types required for their operation.

Admission policies can restrict or deny unsafe volume types and validate how volumes are configured before a pod is created." tags="level-1 pri-2 Workload Workload.Volume _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod" slug="Volumes" help.log.hostpath_rejected="# Pod log-collector mounts the node's /var/log with a hostPath volume
$ kubectl create -f log-collector.yaml
Error from server (Forbidden): error when creating "log-collector.yaml": pods "log-collector" is forbidden: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy 'deny-hostpath-volumes' with binding 'deny-hostpath-volumes' denied request: hostPath volumes are not allowed: host-logs" help.yaml.deny_hostpath_volumes="# Rejects pods with hostPath volumes in every namespace except kube-system
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
 name: deny-hostpath-volumes
spec:
 failurePolicy: Fail
 matchConstraints:
 resourceRules:
 - apiGroups: [""]
 apiVersions: ["v1"]
 operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
 resources: ["pods"]
 validations:
 - expression: "object.spec.?volumes.orValue([]).all(v, !has(v.hostPath))"
 messageExpression: "'hostPath volumes are not allowed: ' + object.spec.volumes.filter(v, has(v.hostPath)).map(v, v.name).join(', ')"
 reason: Forbidden
---
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding
metadata:
 name: deny-hostpath-volumes
spec:
 policyName: deny-hostpath-volumes
 validationActions: ["Deny"]
 matchResources:
 namespaceSelector:
 matchExpressions:
 - key: kubernetes.io/metadata.name
 operator: NotIn
 values: ["kube-system"]"/>
g.data-help:
Volume definitions
Pods can use different volume types, some of which may expose sensitive host resources to containers.
Volume types such as hostPath can provide direct access to the node filesystem and are commonly restricted in security-sensitive environments. Workloads should only be allowed to use volume types required for their operation.
Admission policies can restrict or deny unsafe volume types and validate how volumes are configured before a pod is created.
g.data-help.log.hostpath_rejected: # Pod log-collector mounts the node's /var/log with a hostPath volume $ kubectl create -f log-collector.yaml Error from server (Forbidden): error when creating "log-collector.yaml": pods "log-collector" is forbidden: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy 'deny-hostpath-volumes' with binding 'deny-hostpath-volumes' denied request: hostPath volumes are not allowed: host-logs
g.data-help.yaml.deny_hostpath_volumes: # Rejects pods with hostPath volumes in every namespace except kube-system apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1 kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy metadata: name: deny-hostpath-volumes spec: failurePolicy: Fail matchConstraints: resourceRules: - apiGroups: [""] apiVersions: ["v1"] operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"] resources: ["pods"] validations: - expression: "object.spec.?volumes.orValue([]).all(v, !has(v.hostPath))" messageExpression: "'hostPath volumes are not allowed: ' + object.spec.volumes.filter(v, has(v.hostPath)).map(v, v.name).join(', ')" reason: Forbidden --- apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1 kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding metadata: name: deny-hostpath-volumes spec: policyName: deny-hostpath-volumes validationActions: ["Deny"] matchResources: namespaceSelector: matchExpressions: - key: kubernetes.io/metadata.name operator: NotIn values: ["kube-system"]

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b>?</b></font>" help="Kubelet and API Server Communication

The kubelet is the Kubernetes agent running on each worker node and communicates directly with the Kubernetes API server.

The kubelet acts as a client of the Kubernetes API, registering the node, reporting node and pod status, and watching for pods assigned to its node. Changes are received through API watches, allowing the kubelet to continuously reconcile the desired state with the containers running on the node.

The API server can also connect to the Kubelet API, typically on port 10250, for operations such as container logs, exec, and attach." tags="level-2 info ControlPlane ControlPlane.Kubelet _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="KubeletApi"/>
g.data-help:
Kubelet and API Server Communication
The kubelet is the Kubernetes agent running on each worker node and communicates directly with the Kubernetes API server.
The kubelet acts as a client of the Kubernetes API, registering the node, reporting node and pod status, and watching for pods assigned to its node. Changes are received through API watches, allowing the kubelet to continuously reconcile the desired state with the containers running on the node.
The API server can also connect to the Kubelet API, typically on port 10250, for operations such as container logs, exec, and attach.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Kubelet API Access and NodeRestriction

Kubelets authenticate to the Kubernetes API using their node identity and should only be permitted to access resources required for their own node.

The Node authorizer limits what authenticated kubelets can access, while the NodeRestriction admission plugin further restricts which Node and Pod objects a kubelet is allowed to modify.

Together, these controls help prevent a compromised kubelet from modifying other nodes, changing pods assigned to other nodes, or manipulating protected node labels that could influence workload scheduling." tags="level-2 pri-2 ControlPlane ControlPlane.Kubelet _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="KubeletAccess"/>
g.data-help:
Kubelet API Access and NodeRestriction
Kubelets authenticate to the Kubernetes API using their node identity and should only be permitted to access resources required for their own node.
The Node authorizer limits what authenticated kubelets can access, while the NodeRestriction admission plugin further restricts which Node and Pod objects a kubelet is allowed to modify.
Together, these controls help prevent a compromised kubelet from modifying other nodes, changing pods assigned to other nodes, or manipulating protected node labels that could influence workload scheduling.

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="font-size: 18px; color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b style="">?</b></font>" help="OCI Container

A container is not a virtual machine, but an isolated Linux process running directly on the worker node’s kernel.

The container runtime creates the process according to the OCI specification and configures its filesystem, namespaces, cgroups, capabilities, security controls, environment, and other runtime settings.

Kubernetes typically uses a CRI runtime such as containerd or CRI-O, which in turn uses an OCI runtime such as runc or crun to create and start the container process.

After startup, the workload runs as normal Linux processes isolated and restricted by kernel mechanisms." tags="level-1 info _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod _.Area.Container" slug="OciContainer"/>
g.data-help:
OCI Container
A container is not a virtual machine, but an isolated Linux process running directly on the worker node’s kernel.
The container runtime creates the process according to the OCI specification and configures its filesystem, namespaces, cgroups, capabilities, security controls, environment, and other runtime settings.
Kubernetes typically uses a CRI runtime such as containerd or CRI-O, which in turn uses an OCI runtime such as runc or crun to create and start the container process.
After startup, the workload runs as normal Linux processes isolated and restricted by kernel mechanisms.

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b>?</b></font>" help="Scheduler & Controller Manager > API Server

The kube-scheduler and kube-controller-manager act as clients of the Kubernetes API and initiate authenticated HTTPS connections to the API server.

Both use list/watch requests to continuously observe cluster state and write changes back through the API. The scheduler assigns pods to nodes, while the controller-manager reconciles resources toward their desired state.

All requests are authenticated and authorized by the API server. Neither component accesses etcd directly." tags="level-2 info Api ControlPlane _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="CoreToApi"/>
g.data-help:
Scheduler & Controller Manager > API Server
The kube-scheduler and kube-controller-manager act as clients of the Kubernetes API and initiate authenticated HTTPS connections to the API server.
Both use list/watch requests to continuously observe cluster state and write changes back through the API. The scheduler assigns pods to nodes, while the controller-manager reconciles resources toward their desired state.
All requests are authenticated and authorized by the API server. Neither component accesses etcd directly.
